articles.title: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari - NST Online
articles.summary: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari  NST Online
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's exports to the United States surged 69.1 per cent to RM282.07 billion in the first nine months of this year, despite additional US tariffs on some Malaysian goods.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said total trade between Malaysia and the US rose 39.6 per cent to RM378.70 billion from January to September.
"This strong export performance was driven mainly by a surge in demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products, particularly semiconductors, following the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data centres," Johari said in a written parliamentary reply.
He was responding to Amirudin Shari (PH-Gombak), who asked about the impact of US tariffs on Malaysian industries this year and efforts to identify new markets for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
Johari said Malaysia had also benefited from an exemption from additional US tariffs on most semiconductor and E&E products.
What To Read Next
"This decision by the US underscores the reliance of the US supply chain on the E&E sector."
The E&E sector accounts for about 64.2 per cent of Malaysia's exports to the US, with semiconductors making up 44 per cent of E&E exports.
Johari said the ministry had identified products heavily reliant on the US market that were subject to additional tariffs and did not qualify for exemptions.
The US accounts for about 32 to 47 per cent of Malaysia's exports of rubber gloves, furniture and medical devices.
Exports of rubber gloves to the US fell 1.6 per cent to RM5 billion from RM5.1 billion a year earlier.
Furniture exports declined 19.2 per cent to RM3.77 billion from RM4.67 billion, while medical device exports dropped 12 per cent to RM8.74 billion from RM9.93 billion.
He said some key industries had come under pressure to absorb additional tariff costs or offer discounts to buyers to remain competitive and retain access to the US market.
Diversifying export destinations and reducing reliance on any single market remained the best way to limit exposure to external shocks, he said.
The ministry was pursuing free trade agreements and exploring non-traditional markets in the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
It was also supporting SMEs through grants, incentives and trade and investment missions.
Malaysia's rubber glove exports recorded growth in several non-traditional markets, including Oman (712 per cent), Brazil (84.6 per cent), Sweden (80.8 per cent), Denmark (48.1 per cent), the Netherlands (43.7 per cent), Estonia (34 per cent) and Canada (18.4 per cent).
Medical device exports also increased in South Korea (206 per cent), Singapore (74.9 per cent), Sweden (65 per cent), Brazil (59.1 per cent), Türkiye (43.9 per cent), Canada (26.6 per cent) and the United Kingdom (5 per cent).
Furniture exports rose sharply in Guyana (586.1 per cent), Taiwan (140 per cent), Switzerland (135.4 per cent), Vietnam (99 per cent) and New Zealand (68.3 per cent).
Johari said the ministry would keep monitoring US trade policy and act proactively to protect exporters and reduce the tariff impact on SMEs.
The US imposed an additional 10 per cent tariff on nearly all Malaysian exports on July 24 after a Section 301 investigation into forced-labour allegations.
Tariff rates from a separate US probe into industrial excess capacity have yet to be determined.

articles.title: Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Throughout its year as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Philippines has aggressively sought to push the China-ASEAN Code of Conduct (CoC) for the South China Sea to the top of the regional agenda and end the long and drawn out diplomatic saga, which dates back more than two decades.
The CoC is part of a long (and thus far inconclusive) quest to find peaceful resolutions to the many maritime and territorial disputes that persistently plague the sea lines of communications across a waterway that accounts for almost a quarter of world trade. A CoC would enable ASEAN to negotiate with China as a united entity, and after all that is what ASEAN is supposed to be all about: a centrist political and trade bloc that can represent the interests of 11 Southeast Asian states on the world stage through a rules based order.
It’s a process that does not suit China, which has done its best to belittle and intimidate Manila and specifically Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who has demanded respect for international law while juggling heated diplomatic tensions and the ASEAN chair. Publicly, Beijing maintains its policy of non-interference and at times even espouses the virtues of potentially resolving maritime issues with Southeast Asian states through ASEAN. But behind the public spotlight, China has persistently used its proxies to obstruct and scuttle the CoC.
Cambodia was particularly useful in this regard. At the 2012 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, hosted by Phnom Penh, Prime Minister Hun Sen was signaling a significant shift in foreign policy toward China and the CoC was topping the agenda. The Philippines and Vietnam pushed to explicitly mention the ongoing Scarborough Shoal standoff and Chinese maritime encroachment in their Exclusive Economic Zones, but Hun Sen and his Foreign Minister Hor Namhong balked and declared that such disputes should be handled bilaterally.
For the first time in ASEAN history, no joint communique was issued at the end of the meeting. It was a major embarrassment for the Cambodians.
The CoC was effectively frozen, delays amid the COVID-19 pandemic followed, and whenever necessary Cambodia could be relied upon to do China’s bidding and scuttle the process.
That is what China wants; bilateral negotiations between individual states that enable it to reject international verdicts like the 2016 arbitral ruling on the South China Sea while protecting its expansive unilateral claims and military bases on artificial reefs.
China has also secured its state, military, and civilian investments along Cambodia’s limited coastline, but times have changed with the roaring days of the Belt and Road Initiative disappearing into the vacuum of history.
Given the colossal damage caused by online scam compounds, Beijing would prefer to exact penance out of Phnom Penh than scout for new investments, and the Cambodians, sources in ASEAN are saying, are not prepared to weather the diplomatic heat from blocking another effort to resolve the CoC.
Thus Beijing has considered and pressed its alternatives ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit, to be held in Manila on November 16–18 and chaired by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Myanmar could work, but it remains barred from ASEAN summits in retaliation for the ousting of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in early 2021 by a junta led by current regime president Min Aung Hlaing. That could change next year.
Timor-Leste, ASEAN sources say, is moving rapidly into China’s orbit, but as the newest member remains unwilling to upset Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, or Singapore on the CoC, nor to offend Cambodia after it shepherded Dili into the trade bloc.
That leaves landlocked Laos, an economic basket case in a region struggling for growth, and an absolute dependent on Chinese largesse. There are shades of the Khmer-Sino relationship from a decade ago now emerging between Vientiane and Beijing.
Late last month, China and Laos announced the opening of a Military Joint Support and Training base north of Vientiane, which has already earned comparisons with China’s development of the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia. Joint military exercises known as “Peace Train 2026” were held in September.
“Cambodia does not have the appetite for this,” said a Western source privy to CoC negotiations between ASEAN states over the last 12 months.
“It’s overwhelmed by the mess created by organized crime, the scam compounds and the conflict with Thailand. Phnom Penh is now moving closer to the United States and it just can’t deal with any more pressure. Myanmar, not yet; Timor-Leste, watch this space.
“Laos? Laos has been tapped by China and will have to defend its interests, and it’s the only country in ASEAN that Beijing can lean on, and it has been doing precisely that. Laos is going to shatter the Philippine dream of using the chair to pass the Code of Conduct. It’s as simple as that.”

articles.title: Asean envoy to visit Myanmar Wednesday, says Thai foreign minister - Free Malaysia Today
articles.summary: Asean envoy to visit Myanmar Wednesday, says Thai foreign minister  Free Malaysia Today
articles.full_text:
There was no immediate indication of whether she would meet with former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been detained in Myanmar since being ousted in a 2021 military coup.
Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow — whose country is a member of the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) — told reporters in Bangkok on Tuesday that the itinerary “is being worked out”.
Lazaro said in July she would visit Myanmar this year in an effort to expand access to humanitarian assistance in the country, which was plunged into civil war by the coup led by military chief turned civilian president Min Aung Hlaing.
Asean chair the Philippines had earlier this year requested “brief access” for its envoy to Suu Kyi, but was rebuffed.
In August, Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the first publicised meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.
In response, the Philippines called for the now 81-year-old’s “complete and unconditional release”, and repeated its request for access.
Sihasak said Lazaro’s visit was timed to allow the envoy to report back to a meeting of Asean ministers ahead of a leaders summit.
“The details of her visit, the itinerary is being worked out,” he said at a joint media appearance with his Malaysian counterpart.
“She is going there as the Asean special envoy, and we hope that there’ll be good progress and some progress for her to report on when the Asean foreign ministers meet in Manila prior to the Asean Summit.”
On Thursday, Suu Kyi’s son Kim Aris was allowed to speak to her on the telephone for the first time in more than five years, in a call from Myanmar’s London embassy.
The UK-based Aris told AFP afterwards that his mother had sounded “fairly healthy”, but added: “I remain very concerned about her well-being.”

articles.title: Southeast Asian Voices On ASEAN-China Relations: Pathways To Peace In The South China Sea - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Southeast Asian Voices On ASEAN-China Relations: Pathways To Peace In The South China Sea - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The 15 October 2026 Diliman Dialogues argued that Southeast Asians must shape South China Sea peace and cooperation themselves rather than accept external narratives.
- Speakers rejected a forced China-or-U.S. choice, urging strategic autonomy, functional cooperation consistent with law, and recognition of the economic costs of strained Philippines-China ties.
- Divergences persisted over shelving disputes versus protecting UNCLOS claims, yet the forum produced practical steps on dialogue, a Code of Conduct, incident management and evidence-based policy.
Amid rising tensions in the South China Sea and intensifying major-power rivalry, the 2nd Diliman Dialogues, held on 15 October 2026 at the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in the Philippines, advanced a simple but powerful proposition that peace, friendship, and cooperation in the region cannot be dictated by narratives produced elsewhere. They must be shaped by Southeast Asians themselves.
The forum brought together scholars from China and from the five founding members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), namely Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and the Philippines. Also participating were Chinese Ambassador to Manila Jing Quan, former National Security Adviser Clarita R. Carlos, former Senator Anna Dominique “Nikki” Coseteng, lawyer-politician Atty. Raul Lambino, Filipino Chinese Friendship Association President Danny Sze, academics, and civic leaders. Held during the Philippines’ ASEAN chairmanship, the forum provided a rare platform for candid regional dialogue.
The event underscored the importance of regional agency in addressing one of Asia’s most consequential security challenges. It advanced the central message that Southeast Asia should not merely serve as an arena for great-power competition but should actively shape its own strategic future.
Why Southeast Asian Voices Matter
The South China Sea is Southeast Asia’s immediate neighborhood. Its fishers, coastal communities, and trading economies bear the direct costs of instability. Yet the region’s story is often narrated by actors outside the region.
Former Senator Coseteng, President of Diliman College, emphasized the importance of dialogue, mutual respect, and regional understanding. She argued that ASEAN’s future should not be defined solely by narratives produced beyond the region or by the preferences of external powers. Instead, Southeast Asians must help shape the conversation based on their own experiences, interests, and aspirations. As she observed, dialogue does not require agreement; it requires a willingness to listen, understand, and engage before passing judgment. In this way, dialogue itself contributes to friendship and confidence-building.
In his remarks highlighting the first anniversary of the Philippines-China Studies Center, Rommel Banlaoi, the center director, backed President Marcos Jr.’s “reset” in Philippines-China relations as a pragmatic way to ease tensions. He cautioned that the reset works only if all government departments, including the security and military establishments, support it in action. The reset rests on the view that the Philippines can firmly assert its sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea while still cooperating with China, its “permanent neighbor,” and maintaining its partnerships with the United States, Japan, Australia, and others. He concluded that a truly independent foreign policy rejects the “either China or the US” dichotomy and makes the Philippines a bridge rather than a battleground, and that Southeast Asian voices should shape ASEAN-China relations, including the push for a Code of Conduct during the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN chairmanship.
A Shared Strategic Architecture and the Rejection of False Choices
Ambassador Jing’s keynote address began from remarkably similar premises. He argued that Philippines-China relations have reached a sensitive juncture that demands prudence, balance, and issue-specific engagement. He stressed that bilateral ties cannot be judged simply as “good” or “bad,” noting that while maritime disputes continue to generate friction, cooperation in trade, diplomacy, law enforcement, and people-to-people exchanges remains robust. Calling for restraint in the South China Sea, he urged both sides to avoid provocations, manage disputes through dialogue, and prevent maritime tensions from overwhelming the broader relationship.
The ambassador highlighted expanding trade, tourism, connectivity, and law enforcement cooperation as evidence that the relationship retains significant strategic and economic value for both countries. He encouraged greater Philippine engagement with China, stronger investor confidence, and deeper people-to-people exchanges, while criticizing what he described as discriminatory actions against Chinese nationals and institutions.
On foreign policy, Jing rejected the notion that Manila must choose between Beijing and Washington, arguing that the Philippines can maintain constructive relations with both powers while prioritizing its own national interests. He concluded by reaffirming China’s commitment to regional peace, stability, and mutually beneficial cooperation with the Philippines and Southeast Asia.
Dr. Carlos supported this view when she argued that the Philippines must pursue strategic autonomy and overcome its security dependence on the United States. The logic of her argument is that a country reliant on a single security partner has less room for independent judgment, and that its choices in the South China Sea risk being shaped by the priorities of others rather than by its own national interests. As the way forward, she called for more functional cooperation in the South China Sea, meaning practical collaboration on shared concerns that does not wait for the sovereignty disputes to be settled.
Friendship and Cooperation as Foundations of Peace
Congressman Antolin A. Oreta III, Chairperson of the House Special Committee on the West Philippine Sea, described the accomplishments of the Committee and reaffirmed its commitment to advancing the Philippines’ maritime rights through legislative action in accordance with international law. He stressed that this legal and legislative track goes hand in hand with peaceful dialogue and practical cooperation with the other claimants. His message thus showed that defending maritime rights and pursuing dialogue are complementary rather than competing tasks, and it gave the Philippine legislature a visible place in the country’s approach to the South China Sea.
Atty. Lambino, speaking as President of the Association for Philippines-China Understanding (APCU), welcomed the Dialogues as a place where Southeast Asian voices have a seat at the table and argued that cooperation begins with understanding that comes “from the heart” (mula sa puso), so that friendship between Filipinos and Chinese is built through conversation, shared experience, and mutual respect rather than agreements and official visits alone. He devoted his remarks to technology, especially artificial intelligence, as the force that will shape the region’s future more than any other. Small and middle nations, he observed, have too often been the stage on which larger powers played out their rivalries, and those that escaped this pattern did so by building capability in their people, industries, food systems, and technology while keeping the freedom to choose their partners wisely. He pointed to Vietnam, Malaysia, and Singapore, which chose a balanced and independent course and were rewarded with progress as well as peace.
Mr. Sze, President of the Filipino Chinese Friendship Association (FCFA) organized his message around three themes: peace, friendship, and cooperation. He held that political differences between governments should not damage the friendship between the two peoples, and that the real question is how such differences are managed, whether allowed to grow into greater divisions or addressed through patient and sincere dialogue. He recalled two historical occasions, the 1986 meeting between Vice President Salvador Laurel and Deng Xiaoping and the 1988 visit of President Corazon Aquino, occasions on which Deng proposed setting the maritime disputes aside temporarily while exploring peaceful solutions and, later, joint development. Sze argued that protecting national interests and maintaining peaceful relations are not contradictory.
Taken together, messages by all speakers gave the forum’s central premise legal, strategic, and relational foundations. Oreta emphasized the legal and legislative defense of maritime rights, Lambino emphasized capability, technology transfer, and the freedom to choose partners, and Sze emphasized dialogue and joint development. Lambino’s call for a balanced and independent course echoed the strategic autonomy urged by Carlos and Banlaoi, while Sze’s invocation of Deng Xiaoping’s approach of shelving disputes closely paralleled Ambassador Jing’s advocacy of joint development, with Sze adding the qualification that any such framework must be consistent with domestic and international law. The messages also complemented Coseteng’s observation that dialogue builds friendship and confidence. Together they suggest that friendship is not a substitute for defending national interests but the condition under which dialogue, restraint, and compromise become possible.
ASEAN Centrality and ASEAN-China Relations
Under the provocative title “ASEAN Centrality (?)”, Carlos presented a skeptical assessment of ASEAN’s current condition. She pointed to the absence of a unified collective voice, the growing preference for bilateral over multilateral diplomacy, the constraints imposed by consensus decision-making, the limited capacity of the ASEAN Secretariat, intensifying major-power rivalry, and the reputational costs of ASEAN’s inability to address the Myanmar crisis effectively. articles.summary: Indonesia Trims Gas Exports to Singapore for Domestic Needs  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Indonesia has officially reduced its natural gas pipeline exports to Singapore, trimming flows by 31 billion British thermal units per day (BBTUD) in a strategic move to prioritize domestic energy requirements. The reduction, which took effect in late October 2026, underscores a shifting energy paradigm in Southeast Asia as Jakarta seeks to shore up local industrial supply and support its broader energy transition goals. The move has prompted careful monitoring by Singaporean energy authorities, who rely heavily on imported gas for electricity generation.
The decision aligns with President Prabowo Subianto’s administration's push to enforce stricter Domestic Market Obligations (DMO) for energy producers. By retaining a larger share of its natural gas output for internal consumption, Indonesia aims to stabilize local energy prices, support downstream industrialization, and reduce reliance on coal-fired power generation. The export trimming is expected to last for a designated period, signaling a structural recalibration of regional energy trade flows rather than a temporary supply disruption.
Pipeline Reductions and Domestic Priorities
The reduction in pipeline flows affects the long-standing energy trade relationship between the two neighboring nations. Singapore imports the vast majority of its natural gas via subsea pipelines from Indonesia and Malaysia to fuel its highly efficient combined-cycle gas turbine power plants. The 31 BBTUD cut represents a notable percentage of the daily transit volume, requiring Singapore’s energy market operator to adjust its grid dispatch models and secure alternative supply margins to maintain system reliability.
Indonesian energy officials have defended the reduction as a necessary step to meet surging domestic demand, particularly from the manufacturing and petrochemical sectors. The government has increasingly signaled that future energy resource extraction will be heavily weighted toward supporting national economic development rather than purely export-oriented revenue generation. This policy shift reflects a broader trend among resource-rich ASEAN nations to leverage their natural capital for domestic industrial value addition.
Impact on Singapore's Energy Security
For Singapore, the reduction highlights the inherent vulnerabilities of an energy-importing nation with limited indigenous resources. The city-state has spent the past decade aggressively diversifying its energy import routes and investing in regasification terminals to accept Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) from global spot markets. While the pipeline reductions from Indonesia are significant, Singapore’s Energy Market Authority has noted that existing long-term contractual frameworks remain intact and that the national grid possesses sufficient buffer capacity to absorb the shortfall without disrupting consumer supply.
Nevertheless, the incident serves as a catalyst for Singapore to accelerate its investments in alternative energy sources, including regional power grids and low-carbon hydrogen. Energy analysts suggest that the gradual tightening of Indonesian export policies will force Singaporean utilities to lock in longer-term, higher-cost LNG contracts or accelerate the deployment of floating solar and regional subsea interconnectors to mitigate future geopolitical supply risks.
Contractual Obligations Versus Market Realities
The reduction has sparked complex discussions regarding the enforceability of cross-border energy contracts in the face of sovereign policy shifts. While Indonesian authorities maintain that the trimming does not breach the fundamental terms of existing supply agreements—often structured with flexible delivery windows and force majeure clauses for domestic emergencies—buyers in Singapore face increased procurement costs to replace the deferred pipeline volumes on the spot market.
Legal and energy trade experts note that sovereign resource nationalism is becoming a more prominent factor in ASEAN energy markets. Governments are increasingly willing to invoke domestic priority clauses to redirect energy flows, even if it causes friction with neighboring trade partners. This dynamic requires regional utilities to build more robust contingency plans and diversify their supply portfolios to insulate consumers from sudden policy-driven volume reductions.
Regional Energy Transition and Policy Shifts
The export curtailment also intersects with Indonesia’s broader commitments to peak power sector emissions and achieve net-zero targets by 2060. By prioritizing gas over coal for domestic baseload power, Jakarta is attempting to manage its carbon footprint while sustaining economic growth. However, the finite nature of its conventional gas reserves means that domestic prioritization will inevitably reduce the surplus available for export to neighboring grids.
- Downstream Industrialization: Retaining gas supplies supports the development of domestic fertilizer, methanol, and petrochemical manufacturing hubs.
- Grid Stability: Ensuring adequate baseload gas supply is critical for integrating higher percentages of intermittent renewable energy into the Indonesian national grid.
- Regional Pricing: Reduced pipeline exports contribute to tighter regional gas markets, potentially elevating long-term LNG benchmark prices in the Asia-Pacific region.
As Southeast Asia navigates the complex transition toward sustainable energy systems, the recalibration of cross-border gas flows between Indonesia and Singapore will serve as a critical case study in balancing national resource sovereignty with regional energy interdependence.

articles.title: “Eroding Tariff Advantages and Manufacturing Constraints”: China Diversification Through Southeast Asia Under Strain, With Key Manufacturing Hubs’ Capabilities a Decisive Factor | Policy News - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: “Eroding Tariff Advantages and Manufacturing Constraints”: China Diversification Through Southeast Asia Under Strain, With Key Manufacturing Hubs’ Capabilities a Decisive Factor | Policy News  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Fading benefits of export rerouting as U.S. tariff differentials between Southeast Asia and China reverse
Supply-chain, infrastructure and workforce constraints prompting more production relocations back to China
Success of China diversification strategies contingent on the development of Southeast Asia’s manufacturing ecosystem
Chinese manufacturers’ efforts to relocate production to Southeast Asia have encountered setbacks. The United States’ partial withdrawal of additional tariffs on low-cost Chinese consumer goods has reduced the benefits of rerouting exports, while shortcomings in local manufacturing conditions have become increasingly apparent, including △shortages of skilled workers △underdeveloped component and materials supply chains △inadequate power infrastructure. As Chinese companies begin moving production back to the mainland, market observers increasingly expect the direction of global diversification away from China to depend on the steps taken by Southeast Asia’s leading manufacturing hubs.
Lower U.S. Tariff Barriers Against China
According to a September 30 report by Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post (SCMP), China’s Ministry of Commerce and the U.S. White House recently finalized a trade agreement removing additional tariffs on $30 billion worth of imports from each other. The ministry said more than 90% of the Chinese products included on the tariff-relief list were everyday, low-cost consumer goods, including toys, small household appliances and household sundries. If these goods receive most-favored-nation tariff treatment, effective tariff rates on most products will fall sharply to 10% or less under official U.S. Customs schedules, with some becoming entirely duty-free.
These changes have substantially reduced China’s need to reroute exports through Southeast Asia. Major production hubs such as Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand, which have served as key bases for rerouted Chinese exports over the past decade, have been subject to across-the-board additional tariffs of 10–12.5% since July, following the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative’s (USTR) Section 301 investigation into forced labor in supply chains. A reversal has thus taken hold: tariffs on goods exported directly from mainland China to the United States are now lower than those on shipments routed through Southeast Asia.
China’s Competitive Manufacturing Ecosystem
China’s distinctive manufacturing ecosystem is also cited as a constraint on diversification strategies. Reuters reported last month that “companies that moved production outside China have retained or restored parts of their Chinese supply chains after encountering shortages of skilled workers, underdeveloped supplier networks and unreliable power supplies at overseas factories.” Major manufacturing hubs on the Chinese mainland host dense concentrations of not only final-product assemblers but also suppliers serving each stage of production, including tooling, casting, injection molding, electronic components and packaging, as well as production equipment manufacturers. This allows companies to source replacement components or modify molds and product specifications whenever problems arise. China also has a relatively abundant supply of skilled workers experienced in mass production, alongside robust power networks and logistics infrastructure, including ports and roads.
Some companies have moved production back to China to take advantage of these strengths. Jinqiaofeng, an outdoor furniture exporter based in Hangzhou, for example, opened a workshop in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, in 2024 to avoid U.S. tariffs on China, but closed the facility and returned to China this year. The company struggled to obtain the necessary production equipment locally and could not reliably source even basic items such as screws and molds for cup holders. Jinqiaofeng said that once the cost of shipping Chinese components to Vietnam and then exporting the finished products was included, total production costs differed little from those in China.
Table 1. Factors Reducing China’s Need for Production Through Southeast Asia
| Category | Key Details | 
|---|---|
| Lower U.S. tariff burden | The U.S. withdrawal of additional tariffs on low-cost Chinese consumer goods reduces the cost of direct exports from mainland China | 
| Diminishing tariff advantages in Southeast Asia | Additional tariffs on goods from Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand weaken the cost advantages of rerouting exports | 
| China’s supply-chain competitiveness | Dense concentrations of component, materials and equipment suppliers facilitate rapid procurement and changes to product specifications | 
| Production conditions in Southeast Asia | Shortages of skilled workers and suppliers, alongside inadequate power and logistics infrastructure | 
Mixed Results of Efforts to Shed a Chinese Identity
Questions about the effectiveness of China diversification strategies themselves are also mounting. Some Chinese companies have recently gone beyond establishing production outside China, using localized marketing to play down their Chinese identity. A prominent example is Pop Mart, the major Chinese designer toy company. After opening its first permanent U.S. store in 2023, Pop Mart positioned itself as a “global lifestyle and art IP company,” successfully circumventing resistance among U.S. politicians and consumers. It also targeted young American consumers through its “blind box” sales format, in which buyers do not know the contents in advance, and its proprietary character designs, while pursuing broader local appeal through licensing agreements with major Western IP owners behind properties such as Disney and Harry Potter. As a result, Pop Mart’s physical store network in the Americas expanded to 64 locations last year, while its first-quarter earnings disclosure showed U.S. business revenue rising 55–60% year on year.
The problem is that such strategies do not always succeed. Chinese household goods retailer Miniso, for example, initially appointed a Japanese designer as its chief designer and entered overseas markets by presenting itself as a “Japanese-style lifestyle brand.” Observers frequently likened its image to that of Japanese consumer brands such as Muji and Uniqlo. In 2022, however, its Spanish subsidiary’s social media account described dolls wearing the traditional Chinese qipao as “Japanese geisha dolls,” provoking a backlash among Chinese consumers and a sharp decline in its share price during the controversy. Miniso ultimately issued a public apology acknowledging that its initial brand positioning and marketing direction had been misguided, removed Japanese-language elements from more than 3,100 stores in China, and pledged to revise signage and interiors at more than 1,900 overseas stores.
Shein’s Difficult Path to Capital Markets
Shein, the fast-fashion retailer founded in China, has faced similar problems. Headquartered in Singapore, Shein has presented itself as a global fashion platform while working to dilute its Chinese identity through initiatives such as a pop-up store in New York’s Times Square and a partnership with U.S. brand Forever 21. These localization efforts, however, failed to dispel suspicion among U.S. politicians. Members of Congress continued to raise concerns about Shein’s Chinese supply chain and its possible use of cotton from Xinjiang, while in 2023 Republican attorneys general from 16 states called on the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to investigate whether forced labor was present in the company’s supply chain.
These controversies also affected Shein’s access to capital markets. The company pursued a New York stock market listing in 2023 but shifted its plans to London after encountering political opposition in the United States. The British Parliament, however, also scrutinized labor conditions in Shein’s overseas supply chain, while its Chinese ties and supply-chain issues remained obstacles during the listing review. After repeatedly being rebuffed in Western markets, Shein ultimately turned to Hong Kong, where it listed last month at a substantially reduced valuation. The company was valued at $100 billion in a private funding round in 2022, but its valuation fell to $64 billion–$66 billion in 2023–2024. At its Hong Kong listing, Shein was valued at $26.5 billion, more than 70% below its peak.
Southeast Asia’s Industrial Capabilities Put to the Test
As corporate strategies to diversify away from China lose momentum, experts expect the actions of Southeast Asia’s major manufacturing hubs to determine the direction of the market. They argue that further strengthening the region’s manufacturing ecosystems is essential, as low-cost labor and tariff avoidance alone cannot retain global corporate investment over the long term. Vietnam provides a leading example supporting this assessment. After U.S. trade barriers against China rose, Vietnam absorbed demand for expanded production facilities from Samsung Electronics and Apple suppliers Foxconn and Luxshare, emerging as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the “China plus one” (China+1) strategy. According to the Vietnamese government, registered foreign direct investment (FDI) reached $38.23 billion in 2024, with manufacturing and processing accounting for $25.58 billion, or 66.9% of the total. Vietnam’s trade surplus with the United States also exceeded $123 billion that year, setting a record.
For this investment expansion to translate into meaningful diversification away from China, however, Vietnam must move beyond its role as an assembly base. The visit will also focus on advancing a free, open and inclusive order in the vast Indo-Pacific region, the officials said.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh will seek to strengthen defence ties with Southeast Asian nations and identify new areas of cooperation during his two-day visit to the Philippines for the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus from October 28-29, officials said.
The visit comes days after Singh said India was ready to explore defence cooperation with the Southeast Asian bloc in areas ranging from patrol vessels, radars and air defence systems to helicopters, drones and other technologies.
The visit will also focus on advancing a free, open and inclusive order in the vast Indo-Pacific region, the officials said.
“India is firmly committed to ASEAN centrality and the peace, stability, and collective growth of the Indo-Pacific region under our Act East Policy,” Singh said on the eve of his visit.
“During my visit, I will also hold several bilateral meetings with my counterparts from participating nations. These interactions will be a great opportunity to review our ongoing defence ties and explore new avenues to strengthen our strategic partnerships.”
Also Read: 18 months after Operation Sindoor, India invites Pakistan for SCO event in Delhi
11 ASEAN members, 8 dialogue partners to come together
The ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) is the highest defence consultative and cooperative mechanism in ASEAN. The ADMM-Plus brings together the 11 ASEAN member states—Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam—and eight dialogue partners—India, the US, China, Russia, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand—to strengthen security and defence cooperation.
India has stepped up defence cooperation with ASEAN. Indonesia is set to become the third ASEAN member state, after the Philippines and Vietnam, to acquire the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile jointly developed by India and Russia. The missile proved its lethality during last year’s conflict with Pakistan.
India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries can make their own choices, protect their interests, and pursue development in peace, Singh said on October 14 at the inaugural session of the ASEAN-India Defence Think Tank Forum at the Manohar Parrikar Institute of Defence Studies and Analyses.
Also Read: India set to corner Pakistan on Masood Azhar issue at FATF meet
“We believe that security is strengthened when countries build capacity together, respect international law, and maintain trust through dialogue," Singh said.
His comments also assume significance because China has been looking to boost its influence in the Indo-Pacific by setting up military bases, pushing smaller countries to advance its maritime claims, and forcing strategic concessions from vulnerable States.
India has consistently called for a free, open and inclusive order in the Indo-Pacific, pivoting on respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all nations, while stressing the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue and under the framework of international law. China has longstanding territorial disputes in the South China Sea with several members of the bloc, including Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam.
Singh earlier called for adherence to international law and peaceful resolution of differences. “Differences should be discussed early and peacefully, before they become disputes. We should support a regional order in which countries can work together without being forced to choose sides.”
The Philippines is the chair of ADMM-Plus for 2026. Under the construct of ADMM-Plus, India is co-chairing the experts working group on counter-terrorism with Malaysia for 2024-2027.

Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – A thematic session entitled “Repositioning Vietnam and ASEAN in Global Value Chains” was held on October 27 as part of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, organised by the Ho Chi Minh City People’s Committee in co-branding with the World Economic Forum. 
Participants discussed challenges and solutions to strengthen the region and Vietnam’s resilience and future readiness. 
ASEAN’s potential and challenges 
Nguyen Thuy Lam Tuyen, General Director, Board Chairwoman and Country Holding Officer of ABB Vietnam, said ASEAN is becoming increasingly attractive thanks to its market of more than 680 million people, rapid urbanisation and growing demand for electrification and digital infrastructure. 
The region’s manufacturing investment, digital transformation and automation, together with its young workforce and engineering talent, are further strengthening its competitiveness. In addition, ASEAN has one of the world’s most extensive networks of regional economic partnership agreements. ASEAN connectivity goes beyond links among its 11 member states to form an integrated production base. Each country has its own identity and strengths, which together enhance the region’s overall appeal and competitiveness. 
Sacha Dray, an economist at the World Bank in Economic Policy Unit for Vietnam, noted that ASEAN has a combined economic value of around 4 trillion USD and is expected to become the world’s fifth-largest economic bloc in 2027. The region attracts more than 15% of global foreign direct investment (FDI) annually, supported by trade openness, a workforce of over 370 million and extensive free trade agreements. 
However, intra-regional trade accounts for only 22% of ASEAN’s annual exports of 2 trillion USD, compared with around 60% of goods produced and consumed within the European Union. This leaves ASEAN more exposed to external demand and limits the benefits of deeper regional integration, Dray said. Despite being well integrated into global value chains, the bloc still has considerable room to develop supply chains within the region. 
Strengthening regional cooperation 
Participants stressed the need to leverage each member’s strengths and build complementary links across global value chains. 
Tuyen proposed establishing regional capability corridors based on specialisation, diversification and connectivity, alongside greater sharing of skills and technology. ASEAN should move beyond participating in global supply chains to helping shape them, with engineering and innovation serving as key drivers. 
Pham Quynh Mai, Deputy Director of the Ministry of Industry and Trade’s Department of Foreign Market Development and Multilateral Trade Policy, called for cross-border industrial clusters connecting major corporations, small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), universities and research centres, particularly in electronics, semiconductors, automobiles and clean energy. Such clusters could attract investment, facilitate technology transfer, strengthen supply chains and promote balanced, sustainable development. 
Dray said ASEAN should focus on helping companies become more capable suppliers and meet evolving environmental, social and governance (ESG) requirements. He cited World Bank support for LG’s 200-million-USD project in Hai Phong to ensure that its third factory in Vietnam uses 100% renewable energy, and help local firms upgrade to become first- and second-tier suppliers. 
He also urged greater cross-border investment, trade promotion within ASEAN, support for SMEs and the removal of non-tariff barriers through trade facilitation, single-window mechanisms, and harmonised standards. 
Participants agreed that Vietnam and other ASEAN members have the potential to move up global value chains. Achieving this will require deeper regional cooperation, stronger technological capabilities and better use of each member’s comparative advantages./.

articles.summary: Strengthening FDI linkages creates room for the development of supporting industries.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Foreign direct investment (FDI) continues to increase in the processing and manufacturing industries, opening up opportunities for supporting industries. Increased linkages and supply chain capacity help Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in the supply chain.
The large gap between Vietnamese suppliers and FDI suppliers.
The wave of manufacturing relocation and supply chain diversification strategies by multinational corporations is opening up opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in global supply chains. However, attracting large corporations does not automatically mean that domestic businesses become supply partners.
In reality, the gap between domestic supporting industries and multinational corporations remains significant. According to statistics, out of approximately 1,000 enterprises capable of directly supplying assembly companies and multinational corporations, domestic enterprises account for only about 30%. Meanwhile, about 88% of supporting industry enterprises are small and medium-sized, largely limited in terms of capital, technology, management capacity, and access to market information.
Sharing her views on this matter, Ms. Truong Thi Chi Binh, General Secretary of the Vietnam Association of Supporting Industries (VASI) , stated : Vietnamese businesses are still lacking and weak, making it difficult for them to participate in the supply chains of FDI (foreign direct investment) enterprises because these corporations usually already have stable supplier networks. Domestic businesses wanting to become alternative suppliers must compete on price and quality. Therefore, advantages in labor costs or geographical distance are not enough for Vietnamese businesses to win orders. To participate directly, businesses must demonstrate stable production capacity, the ability to meet technical standards, and long-term economic efficiency.
According to the assessment of the Department of Industry ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), despite achieving positive results, Vietnam's supporting industries still face many limitations, especially in terms of mechanisms, policies, production capacity, and self-sufficiency in supply. The majority of businesses are small in scale, with limited technological and management capabilities, and lack specialized technical support centers, resulting in FDI enterprises' ability to participate in supply chains not being commensurate with their potential.
You may also like
Policies to promote linkages and develop domestic suppliers.
To become a supplier for large corporations, businesses need not only the capacity to manufacture components but also the ability to simultaneously meet stringent requirements regarding quality, stability, delivery schedules, traceability, and continuous improvement. For high-tech components, the supplier evaluation and selection process requires significant time, resources, and technical expertise.
More importantly, the effectiveness of supporting industry development programs needs to be evaluated by concrete results, such as the number of businesses becoming new suppliers, the percentage of products meeting international standards, the value of orders fulfilled, and the level of technological capacity increase of Vietnamese businesses. This forms the basis for determining the actual transformation in the relationship between FDI enterprises and the domestic manufacturing sector.
Speaking with a reporter from the Industry and Trade Newspaper, Mr. Chu Viet Cuong, from the Supporting Industries Department of the Industry Bureau, also outlined solutions. For FDI enterprises, attracting investment needs to be more closely linked to the goal of enhancing domestic linkages, developing Vietnamese suppliers, and transferring technology according to a suitable roadmap. Large corporations should also be encouraged to provide technical support, consulting on production improvements, and create opportunities for SMEs to gradually meet international standards. This approach helps shift the relationship between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises from a simple buying and selling transaction to a cooperation in capacity building. When Vietnamese enterprises can consistently meet requirements regarding quality, schedule, and cost, their ability to participate more deeply in the supply chain will improve.
From a business perspective, Mr. Nguyen Hoang, Chairman of the Hanoi Supporting Industries Business Association (HANSIBA), believes that, in addition to the efforts of businesses, the connection mechanism between FDI corporations and domestic suppliers needs to be improved. Domestic businesses need early access to information about component needs, technical standards, order sizes, and supplier development roadmaps. If they only seek partners when their factories are already operating stably, Vietnamese businesses will not have enough time to prepare.
In the long term, Vietnamese businesses need to aim for higher-value positions, from manufacturing components according to blueprints to designing, developing products, and mastering technology. With the capacity to research, innovate, and provide technical solutions, businesses will reduce their dependence on outsourcing orders and have the opportunity to participate more deeply in their customers' product development processes.
Furthermore, the need to strengthen linkages between the FDI sector and domestic enterprises has been identified in Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy. The resolution emphasizes enhancing the spillover effects of the FDI sector through technology transfer, human resource training, and the development of domestic suppliers. Simultaneously, the document sets out the task of developing a national program for domestic supplier development, establishing a database and platform for connecting FDI enterprises with Vietnamese businesses.
Furthermore, Government Decree No. 96/2026/ND-CP dated March 31, 2026, continues to identify the production of products on the list of priority supporting industrial products as a sector with special investment incentives. Prime Minister 's Decision No. 929/QD-TTg dated May 25, 2026, approving the Program for the Development of Supporting Industries for the period 2026-2035, also emphasizes improving technological capacity, quality management, human resource training, and strengthening connections between domestic enterprises and leading enterprises.
You may also like
These policies provide a foundation for promoting linkages between the two regions, but their actual effectiveness depends on how they are implemented and the ability to translate these principles into concrete production cooperation relationships. The development of supporting industries should be carried out in a way that encourages cooperation based on the harmonious interests of all parties, while ensuring compliance with international commitments.
This requires creating incentives for FDI enterprises to proactively develop their supplier networks in Vietnam, enhance technology transfer, train human resources, and connect production. Simultaneously, support policies should focus on improving the competitiveness of domestic enterprises, helping them meet the requirements of global supply chains through product quality, productivity, and technological capabilities.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) continues to play a crucial role in industrial development. Strengthening linkages and enhancing absorption capacity will determine the extent to which Vietnamese businesses can capitalize on opportunities. When investment projects not only generate output and export revenue but also promote the formation of a capable domestic supplier network, supporting industries will have more room for development, contributing to increased domestic added value and Vietnam's position in the global industrial chain.

Jakarta (ANTARA) - Industry Minister Muhammad Sarmuji has urged Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indonesia (TMMIN) to increase vehicle exports and expand domestic battery electric vehicle (BEV) production.
The minister also urged TMMIN to explore manufacturing double-cab pickup trucks domestically to strengthen the national automotive industry.
Sarmuji made the remarks during a meeting with company executives in Jakarta on Tuesday to discuss vehicle production, export targets, and industry growth.
"We have asked Toyota to increase vehicle exports from Indonesia, both by expanding its model lineup and the number of destination countries," Sarmuji told reporters after the meeting.
He cited Australia as a key potential market for Indonesian-built vehicles, noting that geographical proximity and existing trade agreements offer strong export advantages.
However, Sarmuji pointed out that neighboring countries currently supply a significant share of vehicles to the Australian market.
He encouraged the Japanese automaker to manufacture double-cab pickup trucks in Indonesia to capture Australian market demand.
Sarmuji noted that the government stands ready to optimize the domestic automotive regulatory framework to support local double-cab pickup truck production.
"If improvements to the double-cab vehicle ecosystem are needed, we can also work on that," he said.
Beyond export growth, Sarmuji urged the automaker to accelerate its BEV manufacturing roadmap.
He commended Toyota for producing hybrid vehicles and operating a local hybrid battery plant that exports components internationally.
However, he emphasized that the government expects the automaker to take further steps in full battery electric vehicle assembly.
"Why? Because our battery ecosystem is already highly advanced. The government is also paying considerable attention to the battery ecosystem," Sarmuji said.
He praised TMMIN's economic contribution, noting that the subsidiary directly employs roughly 8,000 workers while supporting approximately 360,000 jobs across its supply chain and dealer network.
TMMIN President Director Nandi Julyanto said the company has begun assembling the bZ4X electric vehicle locally and is preparing additional BEV models tailored to domestic consumer demand.
"We are already producing the bZ4X in Indonesia. We are also preparing to introduce other BEV models in the future that will suit the Indonesian market," Julyanto said.
Julyanto added that the company remains committed to expanding export volumes, broadening its vehicle lineup, and entering new export destinations.

articles.summary: “To Canada with Lower Tariff Barriers” Chinese Complete Vehicle Industry Accelerates Local Market Entry, Seeking Opportunities Amid Global Protectionism Spread  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Chinese complete vehicle manufacturers such as Geely and BYD intensify efforts to capture the Canadian market
Canada lowers entry barriers by abolishing high tariffs on Chinese EVs and introducing import quotas
Chinese companies expand influence in various countries' auto markets despite ongoing tariff countermeasures
China's Geely Automobile Holdings has formalized its commercial sales plan in the Canadian market. With the Canadian government withdrawing high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and implementing limited import quotas, the entry barrier has lowered, accelerating Chinese companies' moves to secure local sales networks, infrastructure, and production bases. The market is watching to see if Chinese electric vehicles, which have quickly expanded their sales bases in Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia, can also increase their influence in Canada.
Chinese Complete Vehicle Industry Targeting Canada
According to UK automotive industry specialist media Inautonews on the 15th (local time), Geely Automobile announced its plan to enter the Canadian market in an official press release on the 9th. It has already completed its local organizational structure in Canada and is building sales and service networks ahead of vehicle launches. Brian Wu, Managing Director of Geely Auto Canada, stated, "Canada is the important next stage in Geely's international growth," adding, "We will build strong local partnerships and customer support systems to earn consumer trust." Full-scale vehicle sales are scheduled to begin in 2027.
Geely Automobile is not the only Chinese complete vehicle manufacturer preparing to enter the Canadian market. In June, BYD Vice Chairman Stella Li stated in an interview with Reuters in London that "We are reviewing vehicle models for release in Canada, and actual sales will likely begin in 2027." Around the same time, Canadian Ministry of Transport data confirmed BYD's initiation of import procedures for two passenger car models produced in Shenzhen and Xi'an, China.
Efforts to secure infrastructure and production bases
BYD is also promoting plans to build electric vehicle charging infrastructure locally in Canada. In Toronto, a 'Flash Charging' business development manager position was recruited in June. The role includes △developing strategies to expand ultra-fast charging networks nationwide △analyzing installation costs and profitability of charging stations △finding local partners responsible for power grid expansion, equipment installation, and on-site operations △managing charging station construction projects. Flash Charging is an ultra-fast charging technology developed in-house by BYD, with the latest system supporting up to 1,500 kilowatts (kW) of charging output. In this context, the U.S. green-focused media The Cool Down (TCD) stated, "If Flash Charging technology spreads, it can reduce consumer concerns about long-distance travel and charging wait times, making EV ownership a more realistic choice for drivers who find it difficult to charge at home." They also noted, "Whether BYD can replicate the charging ecosystem it built in China in Canada will be a key point to watch in the North American EV market going forward."
Moves to secure local production bases are also becoming more visible. According to Bloomberg News, last month Patrick Brown, mayor of Brampton, Canada, stated, "About six months ago, BYD inquired about using Stellantis’s Brampton plant to produce buses." This plant was originally modified by Stellantis to produce the Jeep Compass SUV model but ceased related work last year following the tariff dispute between the U.S. and Canada. Subsequently, Stellantis relocated Jeep Compass production to Belvidere, Illinois, USA. In April, Stellantis began early discussions with Chinese EV company Leapmotor, based in Zhejiang Province, on producing EVs at the Brampton plant.
Trade barriers lowered by additional tariff abolishment
The background behind Chinese automakers rapidly entering the Canadian market is the local government's easing of import regulations on Chinese electric vehicles. In January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a trade agreement in Beijing after meeting with President Xi Jinping that included reducing tariffs on Chinese EVs. Canada had imposed an additional 100% tariff on top of the existing 6.1% tariff on Chinese EVs since October 2024, but decided to abolish this extra tariff and apply the most-favored-nation (MFN) tariff rate of 6.1% on up to 49,000 units annually.
The new system has been effective since March 1. The Canadian government plans to expand the annual import quota of 49,000 Chinese EVs by 6.5% each year and allocate 50% of the total import quota to low-priced EVs priced below CAD 35,000 (approximately USD 25,538) by 2030. The intention is to allow limited market access for Chinese EVs while managing the impact on the domestic automobile industry. Along with this, the Canadian government actively encourages Chinese companies to collaborate with local firms to invest in automobile production facilities and EV supply chains.
Table 1. Canada's Relaxation of Import Regulations on Chinese Electric Vehicles
| Item | Previous System | Changes | Implementation Time and Conditions | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Tariffs | MFN tariff of 6.1% plus 100% additional tariff imposed | Within import quota, 6.1% tariff applied without additional tariff | Effective from March 1, 2026 | 
| Import Quota | No country-specific quota | 49,000 Chinese EVs allowed in the first year, expanded by 6.5% annually thereafter | Quota year from March 1 to end of following February annually | 
| Low-Priced Vehicle Allocation | No separate criteria | A certain quota allocated to vehicles priced under CAD 35,000 | Gradual expansion: 10% in year 2, 50% in year 5 | 
Chinese Electric Vehicles' Global Market Surge
The market is watching if Chinese electric vehicles, which have expanded their sales bases worldwide, can establish a foothold in Canada. According to the '2026 Global EV Outlook' by the International Energy Agency (IEA), China's EV exports surpassed 2.5 million units last year, doubling from the previous year. Growth is particularly pronounced in Europe. According to data from European automotive market analyst Inovev, last year, sales of Chinese-brand passenger cars in 30 European countries totaled approximately 795,000 units, a 90% increase from 417,000 units the previous year. During the same period, Chinese brands' new vehicle market share doubled from about 3% to 6%.
Market penetration of Chinese EVs is accelerating in Latin America as well. Last year, Chinese-made EVs accounted for around 85% of EV sales in Brazil and Mexico respectively. Additionally, Southeast Asia is becoming a key sales region for Chinese EV manufacturers. More than half of the EVs sold in Southeast Asia last year were Chinese brands, with local sales increasing 130% year-on-year. This sales growth trend continues this year. Last month, global accounting and consulting firm PwC analyzed that in the top six ASEAN countries—Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore—the total new vehicle market share of Chinese manufacturers rose from about 11% last year to 16% in the first half of this year.
Increasing number of countries imposing high tariffs
The issue is that multiple countries are also intensifying restrictions on Chinese EVs. For example, the European Union (EU) Commission conducted an anti-subsidy investigation on Chinese EVs for about a year starting in 2023 and imposed provisional countervailing duties in July 2024, judging that Chinese government subsidies distorted competition in the regional market. This was the first large-scale trade sanction on Chinese EVs. In October of the same year, after member state approval, the EU finally confirmed imposing additional tariffs of up to 35.3% per manufacturer on Chinese EVs. These tariffs are additional to the existing 10% import duty on automobiles and are set to apply from October 30, 2024, for five years.
Mexico also approved a bill in December last year imposing tariffs of up to 50% on about 1,400 items including automobiles, auto parts, steel, and textiles imported from non-free trade agreement (FTA) countries such as China, which came into effect on January 1 of this year. The policy applies up to 50% tariffs on complete vehicles and up to 35% on many other items. articles.title: Nanning Expands ASEAN Ties Through Trade, Transport and AI - Medianet News Hub

articles.full_text:
NANNING, China, Oct. 27, 2026 /Xinhua-AsiaNet/ --
Autumn has brought fresh momentum for opening-up to Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. The 23rd China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) and China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit have just concluded, the Pinglu Canal has opened to navigation, and new projects are taking shape at the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center.
As one of China's key gateways for cooperation with ASEAN, Nanning is expanding its international engagement through stronger cooperation platforms, improved connectivity and innovation-driven development, while playing a growing role in China-ASEAN exchanges.
A platform for China-ASEAN cooperation
As the permanent host city of CAEXPO, Nanning has spent more than two decades building what has become known as the "Nanning Channel" - a regular platform linking China and ASEAN in political dialogue, trade and investment, and people-to-people exchanges.
At the 23rd CAEXPO, a newly launched AI marketplace drew considerable attention. The main exhibition area showcased frontier technologies including large AI models and AI chips, alongside products tailored to ASEAN markets such as AI glasses, intelligent robots and rehabilitation and nursing devices.
More than 70 companies displayed over 500 products in eight categories, generating transactions worth more than 28 million yuan (about 3.9 million U.S. dollars). During the expo, Nanning also held a series of business matchmaking events covering digital trade, cross-border e-commerce and intelligent manufacturing, helping exhibitors turn business contacts into commercial and investment opportunities.
At the Nanning Comprehensive Bonded Zone, specialty products from Southeast Asia are distributed across China through cross-border e-commerce networks. Supported by trade links built through CAEXPO, Nanning has seen continued growth in cross-border e-commerce, facilitating two-way flows of ASEAN products into China and Chinese-made goods into ASEAN markets.
In the first eight months of 2026, Nanning's foreign trade totaled 65.171 billion yuan, up 2.4 percent year on year. Trade with ASEAN reached 18.246 billion yuan, accounting for 28 percent of the city's total, while trade with Vietnam increased by 18.6 percent.
A new waterway linking inland China with the sea
The opening of the Pinglu Canal on Sept. 16 has added a new dimension to Nanning's connectivity with the sea.
The canal allows vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes to sail directly from Nanning to the Beibu Gulf. For cargo from southwest China heading to the sea, the route via the Pinglu Canal shortens the inland waterway journey by more than 560 kilometers compared with the route via Guangzhou Port.
The new waterway is strengthening Nanning's role as a transport hub linking inland areas with coastal ports.
To seize the opportunities created by the canal, Nanning is planning industrial development along the Pinglu Canal Economic Belt. Upgrades to the Balian Joint Operation Area in the Liujing Port Zone will enable it to accommodate 5,000-tonne vessels, while construction of a dedicated railway line at Liujing is being accelerated to improve rail-water intermodal transport.
An inland port is thus being transformed into a river-sea transport hub, while industries including nonferrous metals, green chemicals and equipment manufacturing are increasingly clustering along the canal.
The Nanning Area of the China (Guangxi) Pilot Free Trade Zone is providing another source of momentum. In connection with initiatives including the "Two Countries, Twin Parks" model and the China-ASEAN Industrial Cooperation Zone, the Nanning Area has introduced 260 institutional innovations, 214 of which are considered first-of-their-kind practices at the national or autonomous-region level.
It has continued to explore new approaches in areas such as cross-border finance and digital trade. Combined with the lower logistics costs made possible by improved links between Guangxi and ASEAN, these measures are helping Nanning attract industrial investment and develop both airport-oriented and port-related industries.
AI opens a new area of cooperation
Artificial intelligence is emerging as another important field in Nanning's cooperation with ASEAN.
At the exhibition center of the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center in Wuxiang New District, solutions covering smart cities, healthcare, education and agriculture are on display, drawing delegations from ASEAN countries for visits and business discussions.
Nanning is pursuing a development model described as "R&D in Beijing, Shanghai and the Greater Bay Area, integration in Guangxi, and application in ASEAN," seeking to turn the city into a hub for international AI cooperation with Southeast Asia.
ArcherMind Technology has established its ASEAN headquarters in Nanning, with intelligent robot products entering markets including Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam and being used in schools in ASEAN countries. iFLYTEK has signed a strategic cooperation agreement with Nanning to explore AI applications for ASEAN markets in fields including education, healthcare and urban governance.
Semiconductor companies such as Xinchen Semiconductor are also integrating chip technologies and production in Nanning, with applications ranging from the Internet of Vehicles to the Internet of Things.
Nanning is now home to 1,552 AI-related enterprises, accounting for 57.3 percent of Guangxi's total.
During the 23rd CAEXPO, the China-ASEAN AI community in Nanning hosted 37 roadshows and matchmaking events and released 42 cooperation needs for AI application scenarios in ASEAN. Nearly 100 preliminary cooperation agreements were reached, involving around 2 billion yuan, including more than 1 billion yuan in intended cooperation with ASEAN countries.
AI is becoming a new calling card for Nanning's opening-up, broadening China-ASEAN cooperation beyond trade and investment into digital technologies and intelligent applications.
From the long-established "Nanning Channel" to the new opportunities created by the Pinglu Canal and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, Nanning is expanding the scope of its opening-up and strengthening links between Chinese and international markets.
With platforms, transport links and emerging industries increasingly working together, the city is seeking to turn its location at the forefront of China-ASEAN cooperation into more concrete opportunities for trade, investment and innovation.

The outcome of the US midterm elections is being closely monitored across Asia, with potentially significant consequences for Thailand’s export-driven economy. The United States remains one of Thailand’s most important trading partners, with Thai exports to the US valued at approximately US$72.6 billion in 2025, led by electrical and electronic products, machinery, rubber products and vehicles.
For Thailand’s electronics sector, the stakes are particularly high. Electronics and electrical appliances have been the primary drivers of Thai export growth, supported by rising global demand for AI infrastructure, semiconductors and data-centre technologies. Thai exports reached a record US$339.6 billion in 2025, with electronics playing a leading role. Any shift in US policy toward China, technology exports or semiconductor supply chains could directly affect and manufacturing activity in Thailand.
Thailand’s automotive and EV industries are also paying close attention. Motor vehicles and parts remain one of the country’s top export categories, accounting for more than 662 billion baht in exports during the first eight months of 2026. Future US trade measures and industrial policies could influence global production networks, investment decisions and demand for Thai-made vehicles and components.
Meanwhile, Thailand’s agricultural exporters, including rice, rubber and processed food producers, remain vulnerable to shifts in global trade patterns and tariff policies. Recent trade data show agricultural exports facing increasing competitive pressure despite strong performance in some processed food categories.
While the elections are a domestic US event, their impact could extend across global supply chains, trade flows and financial markets. For Thai , the key question is whether post-election policies support stable economic engagement with Asia or deepen strategic and economic divisions between the United States and China.

With a proactive approach to integration, expanding international cooperation, and improving the quality of growth, the province is stepping up investment promotion activities in key markets in Asia and Europe. From eco-friendly and smart industrial park infrastructure to processing and exporting agricultural products that meet international standards, Tay Ninh province is gradually establishing itself as a leading destination for high-tech and high-quality FDI, closely linked to the goal of achieving net emissions of "zero".
In the context of increasingly fierce competition to attract investment, proactively approaching international markets, strengthening dialogue and direct connections with global corporations has been identified by the province as a key solution to maximize local potential and advantages.
Identifying Europe as a strategic market, in 2026 alone, the province organized two investment promotion campaigns in the region, focusing on countries with strong technological capabilities such as Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands , Austria, Hungary, and Bulgaria. The main objective was to find leading partners in the processing industry, high-tech agriculture, food, and environmental protection solutions.
By October 2026, the province had attracted 2,157 FDI projects with a total registered capital of US$27.17 billion, ranking 7th nationwide.
In Bulgaria, the provincial delegation attended a business seminar organized by the Bulgarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) and chaired several direct business-to-business (B2B) networking sessions. Assessing the province's development potential before the European business community, Provincial Party Committee member and Vice Chairman of the Provincial People's Committee Huynh Van Son affirmed: “ Tay Ninh possesses an increasingly expanding development space, a gradually improving transportation infrastructure system, a large land fund for industrial development, and outstanding regional connectivity advantages. The leaders of the Provincial People's Committee also highly appreciated the strengths of Bulgarian businesses in the fields of processing industry, high technology, agriculture , renewable energy, and environmental solutions; considering these as suitable "pieces" that can directly complement the needs of developing "net zero" industry that Tay Ninh is aiming for.
At the B2B networking sessions, representatives from Tan Do Group, Vinh Loc Industrial Park Investment and Construction Joint Stock Company, and their Bulgarian partners directly discussed cooperation opportunities and market development potential. Expanding connections to Europe demonstrates the province's strategic thinking in diversifying markets, partners, and capital sources. As a result, the province not only attracts new capital but also gains access to advanced management models, modern technology, and green production solutions.
Alongside the European market, Japan continues to hold a key investment position for the locality. Among more than 40 countries and territories investing in Tay Ninh province, Japan currently ranks 4th in the number of projects and 5th in total registered capital with 177 projects worth over 1.4 billion USD.
At the Tay Ninh Provincial Investment Promotion Conference held in Japan at the end of October 2026 (organized by the Provincial People's Committee in coordination with the Vietnamese Embassy in Japan), provincial leaders presented detailed development orientations and priority areas for investment attraction. The event resulted in the signing of 5 Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs). articles.summary: Indonesia Is Not Deindustrializing, Industry Minister Says, Citing 5.3% Growth  Jakarta Globe
articles.full_text:
Jakarta. Indonesia is not experiencing deindustrialization, Industry Minister Muhammad Sarmuji said Tuesday, arguing that manufacturing continues to expand faster than the overall economy and remains a major contributor to national output.
Sarmuji said the industrial sector grew 5.3% in 2025, outpacing Indonesia's economic growth of 5.11%, adding that manufacturing currently accounts for approximately 19% of Indonesia's gross domestic product based on the latest data available to his ministry.
"In 2025, the industrial sector grew 5.3%, while the economy expanded 5.11%. These figures alone show that the industrial sector's contribution to GDP and overall economic growth remains highly significant," Sarmuji said after meeting representatives of B-Universe Media Holdings at his office in Jakarta.
He rejected suggestions that Indonesia's manufacturing sector was losing its importance in the economy, pointing to continued industrial expansion and efforts to increase domestic processing of natural resources.
"Some people out there perceive Indonesia as undergoing deindustrialization. But the actual data do not support that conclusion," he said.
The minister said Indonesia was expanding downstream processing activities in the mining and agricultural sectors to generate greater value from domestic resources and reduce reliance on exports of unprocessed commodities.
He also highlighted the performance of the country's industrial subsectors, saying 14 of the 15 subsectors recorded positive growth, while only one experienced a contraction.
"Only one subsector failed to grow, namely the industry related to mining and its supporting activities," Sarmuji said.
The minister urged the media to play a greater role in communicating accurate information about Indonesia's economic performance and development, arguing that public perceptions could be shaped by incomplete information.
He likened information to light that helps people understand the country's actual circumstances.
"If people see Indonesia as being in darkness, it means the light of information has not yet reached everyone," he said.
Sarmuji, a businessman and politician affiliated with the Golkar Party, was appointed industry minister on Oct. 1, replacing Agus Gumiwang Kartasasmita.

(OTCID: AIBT) ("AIBotics" or the "Company") today outlined a Jamaica-first expansion strategy for NovaCore Labs intended to bring commercial technology services to selected markets across the Caribbean Community (CARICOM). The opportunity is increasingly cross-border.
