Yet trade among economies within the region accounted for only 8.4% of their 2023 digitally deliverable services exports. These broader Latin American and Caribbean figures are not CARICOM-specific estimates, but they illustrate the untapped potential for providers that can serve neighboring markets.
A World Bank economic update released in October 2026 projected 2.2% growth across Latin America and the Caribbean for the year, while identifying AI adoption, productivity improvements and technical training as pathways to stronger performance. AIBotics believes that applying advanced technology to real commercial needs—supported by trained personnel and consistent service delivery—offers an opportunity in Caribbean markets even amid modest overall regional economic growth.
Private-sector activity also demonstrates the value of an established regional operating presence. In August, global travel retailer Avolta announced a majority investment in Penha Duty Free Group, an established retailer operating across five Caribbean markets. That separate transaction has no connection to AIBotics, but illustrates how companies in other industries are using local platforms and relationships to pursue growth across multiple island economies.
For NovaCore, AIBotics intends to evaluate potential demand in tourism and hospitality, infrastructure and property surveying, mapping, facility operations and other areas where drones, geospatial information and robotics can solve practical problems. articles.title: Asia-Pacific business confidence dips despite encouraging economic indicators - Vietnam Investment Review - VIR

In Asia-Pacific, the forward-looking New Orders Index improved for a second consecutive quarter in Q3 and now stands close to its highest level in the survey’s history, according to the Global Economic Conditions Survey (GECS) from the Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA) and the Institute of Management Accountants (IMA), published on October 21. The Capital Expenditure and Employment indices for the region also recorded decent gains and are now around their historical averages.
“Confidence among accountants in Asia-Pacific fell back materially, shedding almost three-fifths of its huge Q2 increase, although it remains just above its long-term average. Globally, confidence declined only slightly. The fall in the region may reflect renewed Middle East tensions and the rebound in energy prices, but the key indicators generally point to a constructive picture. The resilient US and global economies are supportive, and several countries in the region are important beneficiaries of the global AI boom, with robust investment in the US fuelling surging exports from Asia-Pacific,” the report said.
Geopolitical instability is the top risk priority for finance professionals in Asia-Pacific, ranked first by 24.1 per cent of respondents in the region, compared with 18.4 per cent globally, where economic pressures lead at 24.4 per cent. Talent and skills concerns (14.9 per cent versus 10 per cent globally) and supply chain disruption (9.2 per cent versus 6.6 per cent) are also ranked first more often in Asia-Pacific than worldwide. Several respondents in the region described how climate change could disrupt supplies and services.
“Asia-Pacific’s key indicators appear quite encouraging, with the region being a major beneficiary of the global AI investment boom. Downside risks remain though, including a further large rise in energy prices and what is expected to be an extremely powerful El Niño weather effect. Anything that fuelled a meaningful slowing in the AI boom would also clearly be problematic,” said Jonathan Ashworth, chief economist, ACCA. “While the global economy has shown remarkable resilience this year, downside risks remain prevalent. The longer energy and other prices remain elevated, the greater the pressure on firms to pass on their cost increases, which would weigh on consumers and increase the likelihood of further rate hikes by the major central banks.”
| Jonathan Ashworth, chief economist, ACCA. Photo: ACCA Vietnam |

Resilient economic activity and elevated cost pressures may increase pressure on the region’s central banks to tighten policy: 41 per cent of respondents expect interest rates to rise in their country over the next three months, up from 24 per cent in Q1 and 30 per cent in Q2.
Globally, the survey points to a resilient economy, although downside risks are growing amid the renewed rise in energy prices and inflation, large increases in government bond yields, and tighter monetary policy. Almost 70 per cent of accountants worldwide reported increased operating costs in Q3, and almost 50 per cent expect interest rates to rise in their country over the next three months, up from 42 per cent in Q2.
“There is something of a tug of war going on in the global economy at the present time, with the AI boom a major driver of growth and stock markets, while higher energy prices, inflation and government bond yields are pulling in the other direction. | The Center's orientation is to channel capital into the real economy , primarily to serve the development of Ho Chi Minh City, the Southeast region, Da Nang, and Central Vietnam. | 
 Building investor confidence
 With new development opportunities arising from expanded connections with Binh Duong and Ba Ria - Vung Tau , Ho Chi Minh City has more room for development in industry, services, trade, marine economy, and logistics. This necessitates innovation in capital mobilization methods, linking financial flows with real-world economic activities.
 According to Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee Vice Chairman Truong Minh Huy Vu, the legal framework for the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City has been completed and the first 10 members have been admitted under the holding company model. In November, the city will issue procedures and regulations for admitting investment funds and fund management units at three levels, compatible with the models in Singapore , Dubai, and Hong Kong.
 The center's orientation is to channel capital into the real economy, primarily to serve the development of Ho Chi Minh City , the Southeast region, Da Nang, and Central Vietnam.
 According to economist Can Van Luc, Vietnam needs to mobilize approximately 280-300 billion USD annually from now until 2030, with an average annual investment growth rate of 14%. During the period 2021-2030, the total capital requirement is nearly 1,500 billion USD, of which the state sector will meet about 20-22%, with the remainder contributed by the domestic and international private sectors.
 Ho Chi Minh City alone needs approximately 1.7 million billion VND annually, equivalent to 22% of the country's capital needs, with 70-80% coming from private sources. Meanwhile, bank credit accounts for about 51% of the total capital, while the stock and corporate bond markets only account for 13-14%.
 "Vietnam absolutely must develop its capital market," Mr. Luc emphasized.
 Sharing international experience, Talgat Amanbayev, Director of Innovation and Member of the Board of Directors of the Astana International Finance Centre (AIFC), said that after 8 years of operation, AIFC has attracted $27 billion in investment capital, of which $17.5 billion was channeled through its trading platform.
 According to him, AIFC's success stems from connecting the financial ecosystem with Kazakhstan and the Central Asian region, implementing pilot projects to enable investors to participate in the market, trade, settle, and withdraw capital. These initial small-scale transactions helped AIFC gradually build its international reputation.
 Richard D. McClellan, CEO of the Vietnam International Finance Centre in Ho Chi Minh City (VIFC HCMC), assessed that Vietnam has advantages in terms of growth, stability, and economic resilience. However, in addition to foreign direct investment (FDI), Vietnam needs to attract more indirect investment.
 According to him, VIFC HCMC is building a one-stop mechanism to connect global capital with real assets in Vietnam. Investors can use foreign currency, repatriate profits, choose foreign law for contracts with foreign partners, apply international financial reporting standards and international arbitration.
 Instead of having to go through Singapore, the Cayman Islands, or other financial centers, capital flows can be maintained right in Vietnam. However, Richard D. McClellan noted that this process takes time, needs to be implemented step by step along with the refinement of regulations.
 One hub, two destinations 
|  | 
| By expanding its connections with Binh Duong and Ba Ria - Vung Tau, Ho Chi Minh City has more room for development in industry, services, trade, marine economy, and logistics. | 
 According to Ms. Dao Thanh Huong, Deputy Director of the Foreign Investment Department, Ministry of Finance , the "One Center, Two Destinations" model is operated uniformly according to Government Decree No. 323, with common regulations, access criteria, monitoring system, and database.
 In this model, Ho Chi Minh City focuses on developing specialized, traditional financial products, while Da Nang emphasizes innovation, financial technology, and new financial products. The two locations complement each other, contributing to attracting international investors and financial institutions.
 Marc Knapper, CEO of Knapper Global Advisors and VIFC HCMC Advisor, stated that the organizational structure includes a central Executive Board, two Executive Offices in Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang, and a unified Supervisory Body.
 Notably, the legal framework supporting the center's operations includes specialized courts that adjudicate in English with the participation of foreign judges, an international arbitration center, the option to choose foreign law in appropriate cases, and the application of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) or General Accounting Standards (GAAP).
 According to Marc Knapper, Vietnamese law remains the governing foundation, but the center applies a special mechanism in which specific regulations are prioritized over other laws, with the exception of the Constitution.
 Based on AIFC's experience, Talgat Amanbayev believes that Vietnam's greatest opportunity lies in leveraging the link between its financial center and the real economy to attract international capital.

articles.title: Grab, Wise and Liquid Group First to Back Singapore Payments Code - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: Grab, Wise and Liquid Group First to Back Singapore Payments Code  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
Grab, Wise and Liquid Group are the first to sign up to Singapore’s new payments industry code of conduct.
The Singapore Fintech Association (SFA) introduced the voluntary code in August 2026 to improve transparency and consumer protection across the payments sector.
It sets standards for payment service providers, including disclosing the full cost of transactions before customers proceed.
This covers transaction fees, exchange rates and any mark-ups.
The code also addresses fair advertising, documented fraud-prevention frameworks, data privacy and security, and regular stress-testing of critical payment systems.
Providers Must Assess Their Own Compliance
The code applies to regulated fiat payment services under Singapore’s Payment Services Act 2019, including services offered by licensed and exempt payment providers. Digital payment token services are excluded.
Participation is voluntary, with providers required to assess their own policies, processes and systems against the code’s standards before publicly declaring their adherence.
These declarations remain valid for one year, after which providers must complete another self-assessment to maintain their status.
The code complements existing Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) regulations rather than replacing them.
Grab, which helped develop the code ahead of its August launch, said it is now working alongside Wise and Liquid Group to put the standards into practice.
The company hopes more payment service providers will follow suit.
Shrawan (SK) Saraogi, Asia Pacific Head of Banking and Expansion, Singapore CEO at Wise, said,
“Because the code is voluntary, its success depends on whether payment service providers choose to adopt it. The code encourages payment service providers to assess themselves against its principles and publicly declare their adherence.
Over time, if more providers do so, consumers can increasingly expect the same standard of pricing transparency across the industry—not just from a handful of companies, but as the norm for payments in Singapore.”

articles.title: Vietnamese private conglomerates step up investment in education - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnamese private conglomerates step up investment in education  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Several private conglomerates in Vietnam are stepping up investment in education through different approaches. From expanding school networks and developing universities to applying technology, businesses are gradually building education ecosystems spanning multiple levels.
Big players enter the education sector
FPT Corporation (HoSE: FPT) has accelerated investment in education complexes in various localities, expanding its training network to meet demand for digital technology talent. In late August 2026, construction began on the FPT Education Complex in Dien Bien province, with investment of more than VND648 billion ($25.08 million) and a site covering about 10.57 hectares.
FPT is also preparing to develop the FPT Education Complex in Dong Hoi, Quang Tri province, covering 5.1 hectares with total investment of VND338 billion ($13.08 million). The project is designed as a multi-level school combining general education with vocational training, from elementary and intermediate levels to college.
The successive launch of projects in different localities shows FPT's continued expansion of its education network, with the aim of building a nationwide system covering multiple levels of education. The group entered the sector in 1999 with the establishment of FPT Education, starting with FPT Aptech, an international programmer training center.
In 2006, FPT established FPT University, marking a major step into education. The group subsequently expanded its training system from primary school to postgraduate education. In 2025, FPT Education had about 50,000 university students, with a vocational education enrollment base of a comparable size. The number of general education campuses also rose to 16 from 12 in 2024.
Alongside FPT, Vingroup (HoSE: VIC) has been building an education ecosystem for more than a decade. The conglomerate entered the sector in 2013 with its first three Vinschool campuses in Hanoi. The network has since expanded to 61 campuses nationwide.
Building on Vinschool, Vingroup has diversified into several education models. In 2019, it established VinUniversity, positioning it as an elite university. It also developed Vin Nexus Center, which focuses on education for children with special needs, and the Brighton College Vietnam international school system through a partnership with Britain's Brighton College.
More recently, Vingroup expanded its education ecosystem with VERTA International School in Hanoi. The school plans to offer a general education curriculum based on the U.S. model, integrating artificial intelligence and emphasizing practical application of knowledge.
From its industrial manufacturing base, Phenikaa Group has also gradually expanded into technology, education and healthcare, aiming to build a diversified ecosystem centered on scientific research and innovation.
In 2017, Phenikaa took over Thanh Tay University, now known as Phenikaa University, marking its entry into higher education. Following restructuring, the university gradually expanded its enrollment, strengthened its research capabilities, and transitioned from a university to a broader university system.
According to information released by the group, it is the first private university in northern Vietnam to operate under this model and the country's 10th university of its kind. It currently serves about 35,000 students across more than 100 undergraduate and postgraduate programs.
At the school level, Phenikaa developed Phenikaa School, a multi-level education system that began operating in 2021. After more than three years, it had nearly 1,700 students.
TH Group has also joined the sector, establishing TH School in 2016. After a decade, the school system has attracted students from nearly 30 countries and has been described by many experts as a model contributing to comprehensive reform of Vietnam's education system.
TH School follows an integrated model from preschool through high school, combining international curricula with selected elements of Vietnamese studies. Its program also incorporates physical education and a carefully researched school nutrition regime tailored to the development and physical condition of Vietnamese children at different ages.
Although it entered education more recently, Intracom Group is gradually expanding its investment, aiming to build a training system linked to scientific research and businesses' practical needs.
In July 2025, the diversified private conglomerate became the strategic investor in Intracom University, formerly Chu Van An University, following an acquisition from Ecopark Group.
After taking over the institution, Intracom set out to develop it into Intracom University under a “Business – University – Innovation – Globalization” model. The plan aims to improve education quality, scientific research and technology transfer, while adopting a modern, smart university management system.
The expansion has been marked by investment in a Hanoi campus. In June 2026, Intracom broke ground on the campus within the Phuong Dong Medical Complex. The project covers more than two hectares, with total floor space exceeding 57,000 square meters, comprising 15 above-ground floors and three basement levels. In late September 2026, the Ministry of Education and Training approved the establishment of Intracom University's Hanoi campus.
Building education empires
Unlike conglomerates that invest in education alongside other business activities, Nguyen Hoang Group (NHG), EQuest and Edufit have identified education as their core business, focusing on building ecosystems covering multiple educational levels and models.
Established in 1999, Nguyen Hoang Group shifted its focus to education in 2008, starting with iSchool International Integration School in Rach Gia, An Giang province. From that first campus, iSchool gradually expanded its network to localities across the country.
The 2015-2018 period marked a notable phase of growth for NHG, as it stepped up investment through mergers and acquisitions (M&A), bringing several educational institutions into its ecosystem. These included Hong Bang International University, Ba Ria-Vung Tau University, North American International School, Gia Dinh University and Hoa Sen University.
Through these acquisitions, NHG expanded into multiple educational levels and models, aiming to build an ecosystem spanning preschool, university and postgraduate education. This also laid the foundation for developing different education brands and models, while paving the way for expansion into healthcare and technology.
According to information released by NHG, its education system currently serves more than 99,000 learners and employs 4,600 lecturers, teachers and staff across 36 campuses in 16 provinces and cities.
From 2026, the group also began expanding into healthcare, starting with the 350-bed Hong Bang International University Hospital. According to the company, it is the first private-sector university-hospital model in Ho Chi Minh City.
Established in 2003, EQuest Education Group has likewise made education its core business, gradually developing an ecosystem spanning general education, universities, colleges and educational technology.
According to information released by the group, EQuest operated 25 educational institutions nationwide in 2025, serving nearly 20,000 school students and about 10,000 university and college students. In addition, more than 180,000 students participated in its STEM programs and used the group's educational technology platforms.
EQuest also has international investors, including KKR, Vietnam Oman Investment (VOI) and TAEL Partners. The company says their involvement has provided additional resources and expertise to support its long-term development and expansion in education.
Edufit has also identified education as its core business. Established in Vietnam in 2011, the group has gradually built an education ecosystem spanning preschool through general education.
Its brands include The Dewey Schools multi-level school system, Sakura Schools, formerly Sakura Montessori International Schools, and the Aqua-Tots international swimming school system.
According to the company, Edufit currently operates 15 campuses and continues to expand nationwide. Through diverse education models, it aims to provide continuous learning pathways that combine general education with experiential teaching methods focused on developing students' capabilities.
Whether entering education from other industries or building businesses around education from the outset, these conglomerates illustrate the sector's appeal and growth potential in Vietnam.
The trend is also unfolding globally, in both developed countries such as the United States, Britain, Australia and Singapore, and emerging economies.

articles.title: Ho Chi Minh City seeks new value in international investment flows. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Ho Chi Minh City seeks new value in international investment flows.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City aims to attract projects that bring technology, production capacity, and added value to domestic businesses. Within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, investors proposed that the city prepare infrastructure, improve procedures, and connect resources.
Domestic businesses need to participate more deeply in the value chain.
Within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, Ho Chi Minh City set a requirement to improve the quality of investment attraction. Discussions focused on how to transform international capital into research, production, and innovation capabilities, while expanding opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to participate in supply chains.
Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan, Vice Chairman of the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City (VIFC-HCMC), stated that Vietnam needs to pay more attention to the real value that projects create. The large scale of capital and exports does not fully reflect the technological mastery capacity of domestic enterprises.
Citing figures for the first nine months of 2026, Mr. Huan stated that Vietnam attracted $50.36 billion in registered foreign direct investment (FDI), while implemented capital reached $21.07 billion. The FDI sector continues to make a significant contribution to production and exports, but the economy remains considerably dependent on imported raw materials and components.
According to OECD data cited by Mr. Huan at the program, in 2020, foreign-sourced value-added accounted for approximately 48% of Vietnam's export value. Domestic value accounted for about 52%, including contributions from FDI enterprises operating in Vietnam. Therefore, Vietnam needs to develop research, design, core technologies, intellectual property, and brands.
Mr. Huan proposed that VIFC-HCMC become the focal point for directing international capital into high value-added industries. Priority areas include AI , semiconductors, automation, robotics, digital technology, digital finance, biotechnology, and green technology.
According to him, each project needs to link investment with research, engineer training, technology transfer, and the development of domestic suppliers. The effectiveness of attracting FDI must be demonstrated through the new capabilities of the economy, in addition to the registered and disbursed capital.
Mr. Peter James Opdahl, Chairman of ITO Group Holdings, stated that Vietnam has become a strategic manufacturing hub for the group in the field of industrial automation since 2012. The company is implementing a plan for a new factory with an area of approximately 12,000 m² under the Green Channel mechanism.
Based on his investment experience, Mr. Opdahl suggested that Vietnam continue to develop supporting industries, assisting small and medium-sized enterprises in participating in global production networks. All parties need to strengthen engineering training, technology transfer, and enhance the research, design, and production capabilities of domestic enterprises.
Mr. Nguyen The Duy, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors and Deputy General Director of Becamex Group, noted that the new generation of investors are interested in connectivity infrastructure, technology, human resources, and support services. Becamex is developing smart, eco-friendly industrial parks that link production with research, automation, and training.
The business aims to develop the Science and Technology Urban Area in the North of Ho Chi Minh City into an integrated ecosystem of high-tech industries, research, innovation, and a modern urban environment. Mr. Duy suggested that the city continue to build breakthrough mechanisms to attract projects with high added value.

In the aviation sector, Mr. To Viet Thang, Permanent Deputy General Director and Chief Safety Officer of Vietjet , believes that Long Thanh International Airport opens up more opportunities for the development of the aviation industry, logistics, and support services. He emphasized the need to apply AI, big data, digitize operations, and prepare high-quality human resources, linking technological innovation with green development.
The proposal needs to be transformed into a feasible project .
Collaborative opportunities can only become projects when investors see clear implementation conditions. Businesses in the CEO500 list are interested in infrastructure connectivity, policy predictability, and coordination mechanisms between agencies.
Nick Chong, Head of Investment Advisory for Southeast Asia at Arup Group, argues that infrastructure creates economic value through connectivity. Investors evaluate the overall transportation corridor, logistics, industrial parks, innovation centers, and urban areas connected to public transport, rather than considering individual projects.
According to Mr. Chong, international funding prioritizes projects with feasible implementation plans, transparent information, and clear risk allocation mechanisms. The government needs to link infrastructure development with land use planning, industry, finance, and the ability to mobilize private capital. He also suggested that all parties define responsibilities and implementation mechanisms from the preparation stage. The government, businesses, and development finance institutions need to cooperate to translate infrastructure needs into projects capable of attracting investment.
Mr. Marc Knapper, former US Ambassador to Vietnam, Chairman of Knapper Global Advisors, and Advisor to VIFC-HCMC, emphasized three requirements of investors: clear and responsive points of contact; transparent procedures with predictable deadlines; and stable and consistent policies.
According to Mr. Knapper, many high-quality projects have implementation periods ranging from 5 to 20 years, and the predictability of policies therefore directly impacts investment decisions. The city needs to quickly develop a list of priority projects, expand international financial services, and establish a one-stop mechanism to support investors.
Mr. Ge Jun, CEO of TOJOY Enterprise Services, introduced the strategic direction for promoting a portfolio of five projects in Ho Chi Minh City, focusing on AI, clean energy, construction robotics, and the low-income economy.
TOJOY representatives proposed establishing a cooperation mechanism with the Global Sharing Office within the next 60–90 days. The parties will continue working to clarify the implementation conditions, aiming to transform the exchanges into a feasible project.
Mr. Nguyen Cong Vinh, Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, stated that the value of activities within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum lies in its ability to transform connections into cooperation, ideas into initiatives, and commitments into concrete projects. The city is ready to cooperate in identifying locations, resources, conditions, and timelines for feasible proposals.
In addition, the City has assigned the Center for the Fourth Industrial Revolution in Ho Chi Minh City as the focal point for compiling recommendations, proposals, and projects from the program. The Center will coordinate with relevant agencies to continue working with businesses and investors after the forum.
Mr. Nguyen Cong Vinh also encouraged large corporations to strengthen links with domestic businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises. These links should promote technology transfer, human resource training, and enhance participation in global value chains.

Economic experts assess that, in the context of volatile global trade, the signing of the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA) not only opens up more opportunities to access developed markets in Europe but also creates momentum for Vietnamese businesses to improve their competitiveness and participate more deeply in the global value chain.
The European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Switzerland, Norway , Iceland, and Liechtenstein, are economies with strengths in technology, finance, and innovation, and are not members of the European Union (EU). Therefore, VEFTA adds a new cooperation framework to Vietnam's integration network in Europe.
In the context of a volatile global trade environment, VEFTA not only opens up more opportunities to access developed markets in Europe but also creates momentum for Vietnamese businesses to enhance their competitiveness. The agreement covers trade in goods, services, investment, intellectual property, dispute resolution, trade and sustainable development.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade 's assessment, the average annual trade turnover between Vietnam and EFTA is approximately 2 billion USD. Vietnam mainly exports seafood, footwear, textiles, and electronic equipment; while importing machinery, industrial equipment, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.
Speaking at the Switzerland-Vietnam Economic Forum Hanoi 2026, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung stated that tariff preferences will help Vietnamese goods expand their markets and enhance their competitiveness; while also creating conditions for EFTA businesses to exploit the potential of the Vietnamese market.
Rules of origin also facilitate production linkages and supply chain connections between Europe and Southeast Asia. “In the context of a still uncertain global economy, the Agreement establishes a transparent, stable, and predictable cooperation framework, helping businesses feel secure in making long-term investments,” the Minister of Industry and Trade emphasized.
You may also like
Notably, for the fisheries sector, opportunities lie not only in exports but also in cooperation in exploitation, processing, and technology application. Ms. Le Hang, Deputy Secretary General of the Vietnam Association of Seafood Processing and Export (VASEP), believes that VEFTA opens up opportunities for the fisheries sector to expand export markets, diversify raw material sources, strengthen technological cooperation, and enhance product value.
Among these, Switzerland is a potential market for Vietnamese seafood products in the high-end segment, thanks to its high income levels and increasing demand for quality, food safety, transparent origin, and sustainable production methods.
Over the years, Vietnamese eco-friendly shrimp, especially shrimp farmed under mangrove forests, has established a firm foothold in this market. According to Ms. Le Hang, eco-friendly mangrove shrimp has a unique competitive advantage because its value lies not only in its quality but also in its production methods that protect the mangrove ecosystem, maintain the natural environment, and support community livelihoods. This provides a foundation for businesses to enhance commercial value and differentiate Vietnamese seafood products in demanding markets.
However, to effectively capitalize on this opportunity, businesses need to ensure transparency and consistency throughout the entire production chain; meet standards for food safety, quality, and sustainability; and maintain a stable supply. In addition, businesses need to correctly identify their customer segments and establish appropriate pricing strategies...
Besides export opportunities, VEFTA can also create conditions for Vietnam to promote cooperation with Norway and Iceland - countries with developed fisheries industries, possessing high-quality raw materials and modern technologies for harvesting, preserving, and processing.
While Vietnam has advantages in processing capacity and the ability to flexibly meet the needs of international customers, these two countries have strengths in raw materials such as salmon, cod, mackerel, herring, and other cold-water seafood.
If Vietnamese seafood businesses take full advantage of the favorable conditions from the agreement, they can expand the import of raw materials from Norway and Iceland for processing in Vietnam, thereby increasing product value and developing complementary supply chains.
You may also like
To take full advantage of the benefits from this agreement, VASEP advises domestic seafood businesses to carefully study the tariff schedules, rules of origin, and technical requirements of each market. articles.title: Interest rates are falling, but concerns remain about difficulty accessing capital. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Interest rates are falling, but concerns remain about difficulty accessing capital.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
While a wave of interest rate reductions is occurring across the board, from savings rates to loan rates, many businesses are facing concerns about difficulty accessing loan capital.
Recently, VTDH Co., Ltd. received a notice from Vietcombank regarding an adjustment in lending interest rates for three loans, ranging from 0.5% to 1.5% per year. Specifically, for a 145-day term, the interest rate decreased from 8% to 6.5% per year; for an 88-day term, from 7.9% to 6.4%; and for a 5-month term, from 8.3% to 6.8%. These rates apply to loans disbursed until December 31, 2026. According to recent announcements, Vietcombank has reduced lending interest rates by 1.5% to 2% per year; for certain sectors, short-term lending rates have been reduced by up to 3% per year compared to current rates.
PHOTO: NGOC THANG
Similarly, a small-to-medium-sized joint-stock bank has introduced a policy of reducing interest rates by 0.5% for the first three months on loans with a minimum term of 6-12 months. The interest rate for a 6-month loan is a fixed rate of 10.2% plus a margin of 3.2%; for a 12-month loan, the fixed rate is 11% plus 3.2%. Thus, the bank's lending interest rate ranges from 13.4% to 14.2% per year.
As can be seen, following directives from the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV), commercial banks have collectively reduced lending interest rates by 1-2% per year, with the highest reduction being 3% per year. The SBV's September lending interest rate report shows that the average lending interest rate for new and existing loans with outstanding balances is 8.4-10.9% per year (an increase of 0.1-0.2% per year compared to August). The average short-term lending interest rate in VND for priority sectors is approximately 4% per year, equal to the maximum short-term lending interest rate stipulated by the SBV (4% per year).
You may also like
The average USD lending interest rate of state-owned commercial banks and joint-stock commercial banks for new and existing loans with outstanding balances was 4.1 - 5.3%/year, a slight decrease of 0.1%/year compared to August. Thus, the average lending interest rate for Vietnamese Dong was nearly 11%/year. Some banks applied an average lending interest rate of 11.24%/year in September, with a difference of 4.85%/year between deposit and lending rates.
Regarding deposit interest rates, more than 20 banks have adjusted their rates downwards in the past week. VPBank recently reduced savings interest rates by 0.4%/year for terms from 6 to 13 months, with the highest rate currently at 7.4%/year, applicable to terms of 15-18 months. Cake By VPBank reduced savings interest rates by 0.3-0.5%/year for terms from 6 to 24 months, down to 6.9%/year. If customers qualify for additional preferential interest rates, the highest rate is 9.1%, instead of 9.6%/year as before…
According to Mr. Nguyen The Minh, Director of Investment at An Binh Securities Company, this round of interest rate reductions by banks will be more drastic because the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) has affirmed that it will review the credit growth target for the remainder of 2026 and assign a lower credit growth target for 2027 to those that do not strictly comply, while also requiring them to implement one or more safety ratios higher than the prescribed level. This means that banks that do not reduce interest rates will have their credit quotas for the following year affected.
Businesses are worried about not being able to access credit.
However, Mr. Nguyen The Minh expressed concern about the risk of interest rates falling while customers cannot access loans due to reduced or capped credit limits. Because capital mobilization is currently difficult, it is concentrated on large, key projects; therefore, the proportion of credit allocated to other businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), will be limited.
"The credit growth limit for this year is around 15%, while the figure by the end of September had already increased to 11.6%. Normally, the fourth quarter sees the strongest credit growth of the year, but the 'pie' of credit growth is only 3%, so it's likely that it won't fully meet the capital needs," Mr. Minh analyzed.
Speaking at a recent conference, Mr. Tran Thanh Trong, General Director of Sang Ban Mai Joint Stock Company, reflected that manufacturing businesses often have low profit margins, while capital cycles extend from 6 months or more. Therefore, if lending interest rates are above 10% per year, financial costs will significantly impact business efficiency. This will severely reduce the motivation for production and business activities of enterprises. According to him, the typical profit margin of enterprises is only about 15%, with the most optimistic scenario reaching 17%, but if interest costs are above 10%, it is considered unprofitable. Therefore, businesses hope that lending interest rates will be adjusted down to below 10% to have "breathing room" and maintain operations. In addition, businesses need capital but lack collateral, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), so banks need to study mechanisms to support SMEs with feasible business contracts.
You may also like
Mr. Dang Van Diem, Chairman of the Dong Nai Provincial Business Federation, also expressed concern that access to credit remains a difficult problem for many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Besides the pressure of capital costs, businesses must also meet conditions regarding collateral, financial documentation, and proof of cash flow. Fluctuations in real estate values also affect the valuation of collateral and the loan limits granted. In reality, some businesses with capital needs and viable business plans still struggle to access suitable credit, while lengthy appraisal and disbursement procedures can cause them to miss business opportunities. Therefore, the business community recommends further reductions in lending interest rates, increased transparency in credit costs, simplification of procedures, and greater flexibility in assessing repayment capacity based on cash flow, output contracts, and the effectiveness of business plans, rather than relying primarily on collateral. At the same time, strengthen credit packages suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises, supporting the maintenance of production, recovery, and enhancement of competitiveness.
Based on the practical experience of member businesses, Mr. Trinh Van Hai, Chairman of the Tay Ninh Provincial Business Association, identified three main obstacles directly affecting access to credit: land and collateral legal issues; factory legal documentation; and financial capacity. He suggested that relevant agencies, banks, and businesses strengthen coordination to resolve these issues, complete documentation, and facilitate the flow of capital. Representatives from the Ho Chi Minh City Business Federation (HUBA) also reported that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are facing many difficulties in accessing bank loans due to obstacles related to collateral, financial documentation, and proof of cash flow. The main collateral for businesses is real estate, but its value has decreased significantly recently. This makes it difficult for businesses to access loan capital.
According to the Vietnam Private Sector Economic Report 2025 and the Provincial Competitiveness Index (PCI 2025) published by the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) in March: 75.5% of businesses stated they cannot access loan capital without collateral. This is a long-standing situation, creating a major barrier for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), especially innovative startups that are strong in ideas but weak in tangible assets. The difficulties in the credit system are clearly demonstrated by the fact that the percentage of loans requiring collateral reaches 93.5%. This not only slows down the expansion of production but also limits the private sector's ability to seize market opportunities.

A Chinese tourist was allegedly undressed by a security guard while she was staying at a resort in Semporna, Malaysia on Sept 19, HK01 reported on Oct 15.
The tourist, surnamed Huang (transliteration), had travelled alone and stayed at the resort.
While she was sleeping, a man broke into her room at around 3am on Sept 19, restraining and undressing her.

Huang stayed hidden until the morning when she was discovered by other resort staff.

Police then arrested the alleged suspect, Amir Kahal, at around 8pm that evening.

His case for assault or use of criminal force to a person with intent to outrage modesty is still under probe, The Star reported.
Semporna Magistrate Don Stiwin Malanjum warned during sentencing earlier this month that strict action will be taken against employers who hire illegal immigrants.

articles.title: Analysis | The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse - The Irrawaddy
articles.summary: Analysis | The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse  The Irrawaddy
articles.full_text:
While Beijing’s military‑centric approach — backed by its “three bottom lines” — defines China’s Myanmar policy, the ground reality shows that civil war is not the only source of instability. Alongside the widening conflict, Myanmar’s foundations are being shaken by a deepening economic crisis with historical echoes. The collapse of General Ne Win’s Burma Socialist Programme Party regime four decades ago was not triggered by battlefield defeat, but by economic breakdown — a reminder that today’s regime faces the same danger.
Deepening economic crisis
When Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited in August 2024, the junta was facing not only military setbacks but also severe inflation marked by surging commodity prices. Thanks to Chinese financial assistance, inflation eased after his trip and the kyat stabilized at around 4,000 per US dollar. But it plunged again after military-staged elections early this year and now hovers near 4,600 per dollar.
Starved of hard currency, the junta restricted imports and choked off border trade. The cost of fuel and cooking oil surged, followed by staples such as rice, eggs, and onions, as well as household electronics and medicines. Vehicle prices soared, and black markets reemerged. Domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and livestock industries — reliant on imported technology, seeds, feed, fertilizers, and medicines — were hit hard, while foreign investment also dwindled.
As the kyat weakens, commodity prices are surging again and shortages are widespread. This is not merely a policy miscalculation: the junta channels all foreign currency into military spending, compounding the economic crisis. Without an end to war, the economic crisis cannot be fixed.
Corrupt state apparatus
Another major issue is systemic corruption in the bureaucracy. Graft grew steadily under military rule from 1988 to 2010 but was restrained somewhat by public oversight during the 2010–2020 reform period. But since the 2021 coup, the entire machinery of government — from Min Aung Hlaing and the top brass down to the lowest ranks — have exploited power for personal gain.
Legal restrictions and licensing requirements have become tollbooths for bribery. Payment is required for import permits, ID cards, passports and the right to travel at home or abroad. Importers routinely pay bribes, while ordinary people face extortion by soldiers and police on the streets. This endemic corruption has also facilitated the boom in narcotics production and online fraud gangs.
Narcotics and online scams
Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of heroin, methamphetamine, and synthetic drugs, with output now rising annually as officials, soldiers and police turn a blind eye in exchange for bribes.
Online scam syndicates previously confined to borderlands are now spreading inland. Evidence from Karen State and northern Shan’s Kokang shows that gangs are relocating under the protection of military‑linked MPs, administrators, border guards, police, and senior officials. Even as criminal syndicates elsewhere in northern Shan are dismantled, Muse—the only border town Naypyitaw still controls thanks to China—remains an online scam hub, highlighting the regime’s complicity in cyber-fraud.
In other words, the economic crisis is not a standalone problem, but deeply intertwined with systemic corruption, narcotics production, and scams.
Poverty and social collapse
Illicit revenues from narcotics and scam syndicates have flooded Myanmar, fueling inflation and driving property values to unsustainable heights. Ordinary citizens are bearing the brunt as the country’s economic crisis deepens. Chinese loans cannot solve this problem.
The persistent civil war, combined with entrenched corruption and criminality, rampant inflation, and worsening shortages, has created a dire situation. While a handful of elites hoard wealth, most of the population struggles to afford basic food, leaving Myanmar society fractured and unstable.
A UNDP report released on October 8 revealed that one in three Myanmar citizens — over 17 million people — are already experiencing multidimensional poverty, with another 19 million at risk. In total, about 37 million people, or 68 percent of the population, are either poor or vulnerable to poverty.
Years of conflict, displacement, economic collapse, and climate shocks have devastated housing, healthcare, education, and livelihoods, worsening deprivation.
China’s other Myanmar headaches
Beyond these crises, China must also reckon with four other problems.
First is anti‑China sentiment — which is rising not only among resistance forces but also within the regime itself. Resistance anger is fueled by Beijing’s support for a failing military regime, not hostility toward Chinese people.
For the regime, however, anti‑China sentiment remains a core worldview. In times of political, economic, or military crisis, the Myanmar military often resorts to Burman nationalism, routinely stoking anti‑China and anti‑Muslim prejudice. In this way, it diverted public anger over rice shortages in 1967 by orchestrating anti‑Chinese riots. Today, the regime sponsors ultranationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha to sustain this narrative.
Propping up the regime offers China no protection from Naypyitaw’s deep-seated disdain. This hostility is not incidental but fundamental; Beijing will be forced to confront it again and again no matter how much support it provides.
Second, the regime’s corrupt apparatus continues to protect online scam syndicates, undermining China’s efforts to suppress them.
Third, the regime has closed key border trade gates including Muse and Chinshwehaw once worth billions annually to China. At a time when Chinese goods are cheaper than Japanese or Western equivalents, the border-trade shutdown is a major loss. Meanwhile, talk of opening trade routes with India has alarm bells ringing in Beijing.
Fourth, the regime is seeking to reestablish relations with the United States. While China might accept restoration of normal diplomatic ties, anything deeper would be difficult for Beijing to tolerate given its red line over Western engagement with ethnic armed groups.
‘Three bottom lines’ collapse
China’s policy goal is stability in Myanmar. But by betting on the Myanmar military to deliver it, Beijing has tethered itself to failure. The regime’s reliance on force over negotiations, corruption over the rule of law, entanglement with narcotics and scams—coupled with economic breakdown—guarantee perpetual instability.
Despite Beijing’s support, Myanmar remains mired in conflict and crisis. The “three bottom lines” have not been upheld: civil strife is intensifying, ASEAN engagement is faltering, and international powers are finding new entry points.
China’s core objective — stability in Myanmar — remains unfulfilled.

Brookland Group & Partners Limited, an investment fund based in Dubai and Singapore, has completed the first tranche of its investment in Miza Joint Stock Company, a Vietnamese manufacturer of recycled packaging.
The transaction marks the initial stage of a structured equity investment agreement worth up to $5 million.
The investment comes less than a month after FTSE Russell officially upgraded Vietnam’s stock market from frontier to secondary emerging-market status.
Eligible Vietnamese stocks are expected to be gradually included in FTSE’s global emerging-market indices over the coming year. While Vietnam’s listed market remains heavily concentrated in banking, securities and real estate, manufacturers operating under circular-economy models are increasingly attracting international investor interest.
Speaking to Vietnam Economic Times / VnEconomy, Mr. Martin Doan, Chief Executive of Brookland Group & Partners, said the fund’s investment assessment process began with the business itself, focusing on its competitive position, management team and ability to generate sustainable profits.
According to the Vietnam Pulp and Paper Association (VPPA), Vietnam’s paper consumption rose 10.8% in 2025 to an estimated 7.77 million tonnes, exceeding domestic production of approximately 6.34 million tonnes.
Meanwhile, regulations governing recyclable packaging are becoming increasingly stringent. Vietnam’s extended producer responsibility (EPR) requirements officially took effect in May 2026. In export markets, the European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) also began applying in August 2026.
These developments are increasing pressure on manufacturers to adopt more sustainable packaging solutions while creating opportunities for businesses positioned to meet evolving environmental requirements and international market demand.

articles.full_text:
Following the State Bank of Vietnam's directive, several banks announced interest rate reductions of up to 2% per year for new loans. This has helped revitalize the real estate market.
The market is expected to recover in early Q2 2027.
Speaking to Thanh Nien newspaper , Mr. Nguyen Dinh Truong, General Director of TT Capital Investment Joint Stock Company, said that the project being developed by TT Capital in the South of Ho Chi Minh City attracted about 800 customers in its first sales phase, with about 30% of them making deposits. Although slightly less than expected, it is still quite successful given that the market has seen a 60-70% decrease in transactions compared to the end of 2025.
"Currently, although interest rates have decreased, they are still high, so customers are only willing to buy houses if they have cash or a genuine need for housing. Therefore, the key to the real estate market right now is still interest rates. Both developers and customers are hoping for further interest rate reductions. Although our project hasn't met expectations, the fact that sales are still steady is considered a success in this sluggish market. With the current directives to drastically lower interest rates, businesses expect more positive signs from the first quarter of next year, but a full resurgence will likely not happen until the end of the first quarter or the beginning of the second quarter of 2027," Mr. Nguyen Dinh Truong calculated.
Mr. Vo Hong Thang, Deputy General Director of DKRA Group, also acknowledged that as soon as the central government issued directives to lower interest rates, the market reacted positively and more optimistically. This included banks reducing lending interest rates for real estate. For example, Vietcombank allocated 20,000 billion VND for customers borrowing to buy houses that have already received ownership certificates. This applies to Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and some neighboring provinces and cities. The preferential loan interest rate is reduced by 1% per year compared to the normal real estate loan interest rate for individuals at Vietcombank, with a loan term of up to 35 years.
You may also like
BIDV offers a 30,000 billion VND credit package for individual customers needing loans to purchase homes in projects with existing land ownership certificates, or to build or renovate homes to meet their actual living needs. Customers can flexibly choose one of three fixed interest rate options: 9.5%/year for 12 months, 10%/year for 18 months, or 10.5%/year for 24 months. This preferential interest rate is 2% lower than the bank's standard home loan package. The maximum loan term is up to 30 years, helping to reduce the pressure of regular repayments and allocate resources to other essential family needs.
In reality, according to Mr. Vo Hong Thang, both customers and businesses are eagerly awaiting a substantial interest rate reduction and are hoping for a brighter market future. However, there will be a time lag before the policy has a more noticeable impact, and accessibility is a major issue, especially in the last months of the year. Currently, everything is uncertain, depending on the central government's macroeconomic policies and the global economic situation. If everything goes smoothly, things will improve by the second quarter of next year.
Projects that cater to genuine housing needs will thrive.
Ms. Vo Nhat Lieu, General Director of PROPIIN Institute for Real Estate Project Development Training, affirmed that lower interest rates could create momentum for a thriving real estate market, but the most important impact is not only reducing monthly debt payments but also alleviating the wait-and-see mentality of buyers.
Recently, many people with genuine housing needs and sufficient capital have delayed their decisions due to concerns about sharply rising borrowing costs after the preferential interest rate period. With interest rates stabilizing and trending downwards, this pent-up demand may return, thereby improving market liquidity.

From the business perspective, lower capital costs help reduce interest rate pressure, maintain construction progress, and improve cash flow. However, lower interest rates are only a necessary condition. Buyers are only willing to invest when prices are affordable, project legal status is clear, and credit policies are sufficiently stable. Given that house prices are still rising faster than incomes, a small reduction in interest rates is unlikely to generate strong purchasing power across the market.
Therefore, the recovery process is likely to be differentiated. Projects with complete legal documentation, guaranteed progress, reasonable prices, and serving genuine housing needs will thrive first. Conversely, overpriced products, land plots far from residential areas, or properties primarily based on expectations of price appreciation will need more time.
"The period when interest rates begin to fall but liquidity has not fully recovered could be a favorable time for buyers to search and negotiate. As the downward trend in interest rates becomes clearer, the number of waiting customers may return, gradually shifting the negotiating advantage to the seller. Therefore, the important signal to watch is not just how much interest rates fall, but whether buyers have truly ended their waiting mentality and are ready to commit," Ms. Vo Nhan Lieu commented .

articles.title: When outsourcing production for foreign companies, businesses sometimes only make a profit of 1 USD per product. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: When outsourcing production for foreign companies, businesses sometimes only make a profit of 1 USD per product.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
To escape the trap of cheap outsourcing and reduce risks from external fluctuations, Vietnamese businesses need to shift towards mastering design, applying technology, and strengthening cross-border industry clusters.
This was the message shared by experts and delegates from both within and outside Vietnam at the discussion session "Repositioning Vietnam and ASEAN in the Global Value Chain," held on the morning of October 27th. The program was part of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026 in Ho Chi Minh City.
The paradox of foreign capital flows and the "low" in intra-bloc trade.
According to data presented at the forum, ASEAN has an economy of approximately US$4.3 trillion, a population of 700 million, and is expected to attract approximately US$245 billion in FDI by 2025 (a 10% increase compared to the previous year). However, the level of trade integration among member economies remains limited.
Data from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) shows that the share of foreign value added in Vietnam's exports increased from 33% in 2010 to nearly 50% in 2022, reflecting a significant dependence on imported inputs in the production of export goods.
This dependence becomes even more fragile when looking at intra-regional trade flows. Sacha Dray, an economist at the World Bank's Economic Policy Unit in Vietnam, stated that intra-regional trade accounts for only about 22% of ASEAN's total merchandise exports, significantly lower than the approximately 60% of the European Union (EU).
The cause stems from a supply-demand imbalance due to the significant income gap between the richest and poorest countries in the bloc, creating a disparity in consumer demand. Furthermore, despite deep involvement in sectors such as automobiles in Thailand, assembly in Vietnam, and semiconductors in Malaysia and Singapore , intra-bloc value chains only account for about one-third of global value chain participation.
Citing the example of Vietnam's wood processing industry – which exports to 168 markets – Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association (VIFOREST), stated that manufacturers are facing trade protection measures from the United States.
He warned that the purely OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) model, based on foreign orders, is stifling innovation and leading to fierce price competition among businesses within the bloc. With designs being copied extensively, the price war to secure orders has resulted in net profit margins sometimes dropping to just $1 per product, or even lower.
In light of this situation, World Bank experts suggest that governments should promote intra-ASEAN investment ("ASEAN to ASEAN"), leverage the spillover effects of FDI, and harmonize technical standards as soon as possible to facilitate mutual recognition among member states.
Businesses need to improve their capabilities.
You may also like
Regarding the true value of FDI, Ms. Jessica Nguyen, General Director of ABB Vietnam, affirmed: "Factories and machinery can be purchased and relocated very quickly, but production and management capabilities require many years of accumulation."
Therefore, the measure of value of foreign capital lies in the transfer of core competencies through three aspects: global quality management expertise to the workforce; the ability to solve complex technical problems for local engineers; and the establishment of trust throughout the supply chain with over 1,000 Vietnamese SMEs based on stability, security, and traceability.
Furthermore, the early transfer of practical knowledge into university classrooms is key to preparing a workforce ready for the future.
ABB leaders emphasized that the future goal of the region should not stop at "Make in ASEAN," but move up to the level of "Engineered and Innovated in ASEAN."
To illustrate this shift, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai cited the case of AA Corporation, a Vietnamese enterprise that transformed from a domestic interior design contractor to a master designer and contractor for turnkey projects of ultra-luxury international hotels such as the Park Hyatt in the Caribbean.
Looking at AA's perspective, Mr. Hoai believes the core lesson is to choose the right high-end niche market segment, using unique designs to drive business operations instead of relying on cheap, large-scale outsourcing contracts.
"ASEAN countries have strong forest resources and need to shift from competitive confrontation to cooperation to jointly upgrade their competitiveness. Transformation will not begin without action, and action will not happen if we do not change our mindset. We must be confident in our own capabilities and intelligence before demanding trust from the global market," Mr. Hoai said.
From a technology application perspective, Youxian Zhu, founder and CEO of Black Lake Technologies, cited the example of a Buddhist temple in China that used AI to design unique souvenir products (such as wooden lion statues), then transferred production data to workshops in Vietnam and China.
As a result, instead of mass-producing goods with a net profit margin of less than $1 per product, the factory earned a profit margin of $10-20 per product, even though the minimum order size was reduced to 100 products.
This example shows that, in order to generate profits, manufacturing plants must quickly adapt to flexible production models.
Flexible production and policy support
You may also like
To realize these micro-level transformations, institutional and regional linkage issues have been identified as crucial foundations. Ms. Pham Quynh Mai, Deputy Director of the Department of Foreign Market Development and Multilateral Trade (Ministry of Industry and Trade), noted that the biggest trade barriers today are no longer tariffs but rather issues "behind the border," such as complex rules of origin, customs procedures, and overlapping technical standards.
For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which account for over 97% of the economy, representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade proposed implementing a National Supplier Development Program, establishing a fund to support capacity building for SMEs, and innovating human resource training through a tripartite cooperation model.
Ms. Pham Quynh Mai suggested that ASEAN should soon develop cross-border industrial clusters in key high-tech sectors such as electronics, semiconductors, automobiles, and clean energy. This model would allow the connection of large corporations, SMEs, universities, and research institutes in multiple countries within the same value chain.
The cluster will optimize the comparative advantages of each member: one country supplying raw materials (such as Indonesia), one country specializing in the production of flexible components (such as Malaysia), and one country handling the assembly and manufacturing of vehicles (such as Thailand).
The formation of cross-border industrial clusters not only helps strengthen regional competitiveness to increase its competitiveness with major manufacturing hubs such as China or India, but also creates a boost to attract high-quality FDI flows associated with technology transfer.
More importantly, this is the most substantial leverage to significantly increase intra-ASEAN trade, drawing less developed regions into ASEAN's sustainable and efficient supply chains.

articles.title: Singapore, Germany to collaborate on AI use in industries, step up research on new tech - The Business Times
articles.summary: Singapore, Germany to collaborate on AI use in industries, step up research on new tech  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
The two countries will also work towards strengthening cooperation between Asean and the EU
[SINGAPORE] Singapore and Germany will deepen cooperation in the digital realm, particularly in the development and deployment of artificial intelligence for the industrial sector.
This comes as both countries announced a refreshed roadmap to further bilateral ties and collaboration on Oct 27, after a meeting between Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
At a joint press conference at Parliament House, PM Wong said both leaders had a fruitful discussion and agreed there was much more to be accomplished together under the strategic partnership between Singapore and Germany.
The updated joint work plan covers collaboration in areas such as AI, digital economy, research and innovation, and Asean, among others, and builds on an earlier roadmap from 2024.
“Singapore and Germany may be geographically far apart, but we share many common interests and convictions, and this was very clear from our discussions this morning,” said PM Wong.
“These shared convictions have underpinned our friendship over the past six decades. And in a world that is becoming more uncertain and fragmented, our ties will be even more important in bringing our two countries and our two regions closer together.”
The German leader agreed, adding that Singapore and Germany are “firmly convinced to further develop our strategic partnership, and we are in for the long haul”.
On AI, PM Wong said both leaders recognise the enormous potential of the technology to transform their countries’ economies and create new opportunities for businesses and workers.
That is why both sides want to move beyond digital technologies to work together on industrial AI, he said.
Industrial AI involves the application of the technology in physical operations, robotics and machinery, such as in manufacturing systems and logistics systems.
PM Wong said Singapore and Germany bring complementary strengths to the table to this end.
“At the same time, we recognise that AI brings new risks and challenges,” he added.
“And so, even as we cooperate on AI deployment, we will ensure that this is done in a way that remains safe, trusted, and human-centred.”
In response to a question from the media on whether middle powers can work together on AI to overtake bigger powers like the United States and China, PM Wong noted that a lot of the frontier developments are taking place in America and to some extent China.
Singapore is focused on the application of AI where it has some advantages to offer, said PM Wong.
As a small, compact, and highly connected society where there is rule of law and clear protections for intellectual property, Singapore can push the frontiers of actual AI deployment in healthcare, logistics, finance, and advanced manufacturing.
Chancellor Merz said both countries’ will also work together on AI security, through their newly set up AI safety and security institutions.
Singapore and Germany will also further cooperation in research and innovation, said PM Wong.
In conjunction with the Singapore-Germany Year of Innovation, both countries intend to pursue more joint research and innovation projects in emerging technologies, covering areas such as AI, advanced manufacturing, green technologies, semiconductors, quantum, and space technologies, he added.
He noted that the strong German academic and research presence here – the Technical University of Munich campus opened in Singapore 2002, and the Max-Planck Centres for Data Driven Chemistry and Biocultural Worlding in April – has created valuable opportunities for collaboration over the years.
Amid a more fragmented world, both sides will also work to strengthen cooperation between Asean and the European Union, which marks 50 years of relations in 2026.
“The zeitgeist is turning against openness and trade, our response is not to turn inwards. Instead, it is to work with like-minded partners to build new connections,” said PM Wong.
He said as Asean chair in 2027, Singapore will work with Germany to deepen the 11-member grouping’s partnership with the EU, including by making progress towards an Asean-EU free trade agreement.
Asked about concrete steps towards this pact, PM Wong said it will be “challenging” and “complex” but there is reason for some optimism.
The EU has started to establish bilateral trade pacts with individual Asean countries such as Singapore and Vietnam, and is negotiating more such pacts with Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.
“That gives us more confidence that Asean as a bloc can also make progress in our trade discussions for a free trade agreement with the EU,” he said.
Besides trade, both sides are also looking at how to bring the digital systems of the two regions together, he said, citing Asean’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement, the first region-wide agreement on digital economy governance covering areas such as digital trade, cross-border e-commerce, cyber security, digital identity, digital payments and cross-border data flows.
He noted that Germany was made an Asean sectoral dialogue partner in July, an important step in bringing Germany and South-east Asia closer together.
Many of the 2,900 German companies based here use Singapore as a gateway to access opportunities across Asean and the wider Pacific region, he said.
Chancellor Merz, speaking at the press conference, said amid geopolitical instability in the world, there is “a very good chance of achieving an even deeper cooperation with the countries of the region”.
Speaking in German, he said he was in favour of working to integrate the existing free trade structures with Germany’s different regional partners like Singapore, Malaysia, India, and Indonesia.
“This will open up better opportunities in the region to us and our companies,” he said.
He said Germany was also ready to support the Asean Power Grid initiative, that aims to connect electricity networks across the region to enable cross-border energy trading and enhance energy security.
PM Wong said Singapore and Germany are also natural partners in upholding the international rules-based order, with both countries committed to international law and multilateral cooperation.
He welcomed Germany’s endorsement of the Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defence Exchanges, or GUIDE, a voluntary initiative focused on protecting critical underwater infrastructure like subsea cables and pipelines
Singapore is among the 17 founding members of the initiative launched earlier this year.
PM Wong said it has strengthened cooperation across regions to protect critical underwater infrastructure, which is essential to security and connectivity.
“We believe that countries large and small benefit from a world where the rules are respected, commitments are honoured, and disputes resolved peacefully,” he added. THE STRAITS TIMES

articles.title: Bank executive reveals conditions for reducing real estate loan interest rates. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Bank executive reveals conditions for reducing real estate loan interest rates.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - To reduce real estate interest rates, bank leaders believe that it is not only necessary to lower deposit interest rates but also to maintain market discipline and allocate credit efficiently.
Following directives from the Government and the State Bank of Vietnam to reduce interest rates to support production and business, a number of banks have adjusted their interest rate schedules since October 19th.
According to the State Bank of Vietnam's directive, credit institutions are required to reduce listed deposit interest rates by at least 0.5% per year for terms of 6 months or more, and simultaneously reduce lending interest rates by 1.5-2% per year for production and business activities and priority sectors. Currently, some bank branches are applying reductions of up to 2.5% per year.
This adjustment has not yet been directly applied to home loans and real estate loans. Speaking with a reporter from Dan Tri newspaper, Mr. Vo Hoang Hai, Deputy General Director of Nam A Bank, said that with reduced input funding costs, lending interest rates, including those for real estate, also have more room to decrease.
According to Mr. Hai, for interest rates to truly cool down, in addition to reducing interest rates, maintaining market discipline is also necessary. When banks consistently fulfill their commitment to reducing interest rates, the lending environment will become more transparent, benefiting banks, businesses, and customers from lower capital costs. However, real estate interest rates can only be reduced to a suitable level due to limited capital and the need for banks to control risks.
You may also like
Mr. Hai analyzed that the more abundant the capital, the more room banks have to apply preferential interest rates. For example, with a credit source of 200,000 billion VND or 20,000 billion VND, the possibility of preferential rates will be wider. Conversely, if the available capital is only about 2,000 billion VND, banks must carefully screen projects and customers. "It's difficult to convince the Board of Directors and shareholders to accept selling scarce capital resources at excessively low interest rates," Mr. Hai said.
To create more room for interest rate reductions, many banks have proactively adjusted their profit targets, directly sharing the financial costs with customers. This approach both supports borrowers and contributes to protecting credit quality and the health of the banking system. According to Mr. Hai, when interest rates cool down, the sentiment of those who need to buy real estate may improve, thereby supporting market liquidity.
From the perspective of real estate businesses, Mr. Le Huu Nghia, General Director of Le Thanh Construction and Trading Company Limited, believes that the reduction in lending interest rates for production and business activities has not yet had a significant impact on the market and requires a time lag. Businesses are more concerned about interest rates on medium and long-term loans, capital used for investment, construction, and project development. If these interest rates do not decrease significantly, lowering interest rates in other sectors is unlikely to create a noticeable change in the real estate market in the short term.
According to statistics from DKRA Consulting at 11 commercial banks, the common fixed interest rate for 12-24 months is around 10.9% per year. A survey by the Vietnam Institute for Real Estate Market Research and Evaluation (VARS IRE) at 10 banks recorded preferential interest rates of 8.5-11% per year, but after the preferential period, the actual rate paid rises to 13-15% per year.
You may also like
To support purchasing power, many developers are extending payment schedules up to 5 years, offering discounts of over 10% for customers who pay quickly, or granting interest-free periods of 2-3 years.
Entering the fourth quarter, the Dat Xanh Services Institute for Economic , Financial, and Real Estate Research (DXS-FERI) has developed three scenarios for the quarter, using the 20-25% absorption rate of the third quarter as a benchmark. In the ideal scenario, supply increases by 30-40%, prices increase by 5-10%, floating interest rates decrease to 10-12%/year, and the absorption rate reaches 40-45%; however, DXS-FERI assesses this scenario as unlikely in the current context. The most feasible expected scenario has a 20-30% increase in supply, stable prices, floating interest rates of 12-14%/year, and an absorption rate of 30-35%.
In the challenging scenario, floating interest rates remain or increase to 14-16% per year, supply increases by 15-20%, prices decrease slightly, and the absorption rate falls below 20%. According to DXS-FERI, the market is shifting its focus from increasing supply to creating real liquidity, with advantages belonging to projects with clear legal status, appropriate selling prices, and flexible payment policies.
