articles.title: PM Lawrence Wong at the Joint Press Conference with Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany Friedrich Merz (Oct 2026) - Prime Minister's Office Singapore
articles.summary: PM Lawrence Wong at the Joint Press Conference with Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany Friedrich Merz (Oct 2026)  Prime Minister's Office Singapore
articles.full_text:
27 October 2026
People
PM Lawrence Wong
Topics
Foreign affairs
Remarks by Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong at the joint press conference with Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany Friedrich Merz on 27 October 2026.
Your Excellency Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz, 
Excellencies,
Ladies and gentlemen,
Let me begin by extending a very warm welcome to Chancellor Merz and his delegation.
Chancellor, it is very good to see you again. When we met last November, I said that I looked forward to welcoming you to Singapore. So, I am delighted that you have taken up this invitation, and that you have also brought with you a very large business delegation.
Bilateral Relations
Our two countries share a longstanding and substantive relationship, built on mutual trust and shared interest. And last year, we marked 60 years of diplomatic ties.
Germany has been an important partner in Singapore’s development from our earliest years. Institutions like the German-Singapore Institute of Production Technology and the Rollei Government Training Centre helped to equip generations of Singaporeans with valuable technical skills and expertise, and supported our transformation into an advanced economy. And so for that we are very grateful.
And over the decades, our relationship has grown from strength to strength. Today our cooperation spans many areas, underpinned by our Strategic Partnership.
Our economic ties are especially strong. Germany is one of Singapore’s largest trading partners in the EU. And our Bilateral trade in both goods and services has increased significantly since the EU-Singapore Free Trade Agreement entered into force.
Today, more than 2,900 German companies are based in Singapore. They include global leaders like Siemens, SAP, Evonik, and Infineon, as well as many innovative Mittelstand companies. They contribute to our economy and they use Singapore as a gateway to access opportunities across ASEAN and the wider Pacific region.
We also enjoy strong defence ties. Our Leopard tanks, our Invincible-class submarines are German-made. And earlier this year, we launched Singapore’s first Sentinel-class Offshore Patrol Vessel, also built and made in Germany.
In particular, Singapore deeply appreciates Germany’s longstanding support of the SAF’s armour training in Oberlausitz and our submarine crew training in Kiel.
These arrangements reflect the high level of trust between our two countries.
Future Areas of Cooperation
We had a fruitful discussion earlier and Chancellor Merz and I both agree that there is much more we can do together under our Strategic Partnership. And we have both agreed on an updated Joint Work Plan.
Let me just briefly highlight a few areas.
First, on the digital economy and Artificial Intelligence.
We both recognise the enormous potential of digital technologies and AI to transform our economies, and create new opportunities for our businesses and workers.
And we want to go further – particularly in the development and deployment of industrial AI, where the strengths of our two countries can complement each other.
At the same time, we recognise that AI brings new risks and challenges. And so even as we both cooperate on AI deployment, we will ensure that this is done in a way that remains safe, trusted and human-centred.
Second, on research and innovation.
There is already a strong German academic and research presence in Singapore. For example, the Technical University of Munich (TUM) established its campus here in 2002 – which was the first campus of a German university abroad. And more recently, two Max-Planck Centres opened here in Singapore, the first of their kind in Southeast Asia.
This year, we also launched the Singapore-Germany Year of Innovation.
We intend to build on this momentum, and pursue more joint research and innovation projects in areas like AI, advanced manufacturing, green technologies, semiconductors, quantum and space technologies.
Third, we will strengthen cooperation between our regions.
Singapore and Germany are both deeply connected to the global economy. We depend on open markets and strong international partnerships.
But the world around us is becoming more fragmented. The zeitgeist is turning against openness and trade. Our response is not to turn inwards. Instead, it is to work with like-minded partners to build new connections.
And so I welcome Germany becoming an ASEAN Sectoral Dialogue Partner in July, which is an important step in bringing Germany and Southeast Asia closer together.
And as ASEAN Chair next year, Singapore will work to deepen ASEAN’s partnerships with both Germany and the EU, including by making progress towards an ASEAN-EU Free Trade Agreement.
Finally, Singapore and Germany are natural partners in upholding the international rules-based order.
We are both committed to international law and multilateral cooperation. And we believe that countries, large and small, benefit from a world where the rules are respected, commitments are honoured, and disputes resolved peacefully.
We are therefore pleased that Germany has joined Singapore and 16 other nations in endorsing the Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defence Exchanges, or GUIDE. This initiative will strengthen cooperation across regions to protect critical underwater infrastructure, which is essential to our security and connectivity.
Conclusion
Singapore and Germany may be geographically far apart, but we share many common interests and convictions and this was very clear from our discussion this morning. These shared convictions have underpinned our friendship over the past six decades. And in a world that is becoming more uncertain and fragmented, our ties will be even more important in bringing our two countries and our two regions closer together.
So, Chancellor Merz, once again let me welcome you to Singapore. I thank you for your friendship and partnership, and look forward to working closely with you to take our bilateral relationship to even greater heights. Thank you very much.

The Chinese stock market is undergoing a sharp correction as a series of key indices have fallen sharply, raising concerns about the outlook for economic growth and corporate profitability.
During the morning session on October 26th, the CSI 300 index fell by approximately 0.5%, to 4,060 points. The sell-off affected many large businesses, from electric vehicle battery manufacturer CATL and Kwai Fumio Group to banks, insurance companies, and technology firms.
The reasons for investor pessimism lie not only in stock price movements, but also in the weakening outlook for corporate profits, sluggish domestic consumption, and the lack of sufficiently strong economic stimulus measures.
Market liquidity has decreased, with margin trading balances falling to their lowest level in a year, reflecting growing caution among investors. Concerns remain that China's manufacturing and export power may not translate proportionally into domestic demand, potentially leading to price increases and lower corporate profits.
China's biggest challenge

The sharp decline in Chinese stocks occurred against the backdrop of persistent economic challenges, such as difficulties in the real estate market, weak consumer spending, overcapacity, and price competition pressure.
The real estate market has yet to recover from its difficulties, and local budgets are under pressure due to declining land-related revenue.
Weak consumer demand is making it difficult for businesses to increase revenue, even with large production capacities. Meanwhile, many industries, from electric vehicles and batteries to e-commerce, are competing by lowering prices to maintain market share.
The overcapacity situation creates a paradox: production may increase, but profits do not increase proportionally. CATL recorded lower-than-expected profits amidst fierce competition. Many other businesses are also under pressure from investment costs, falling selling prices, and a less positive business outlook.
Rising prices also increase the risk of deflation. When goods exceed the market's absorption capacity, businesses are forced to lower prices, narrowing profit margins. If consumers continue to delay purchases in the expectation of lower prices, demand weakens further.
In addition, investors are still monitoring the effectiveness of government support measures on consumption and corporate profits. Trade tensions, the risk of tariffs, and technological restrictions are also factors that could affect export prospects and stock valuations.
According to OECD forecasts published in 2026, China's economic growth could slow to 4.5% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027.
What risks are the Chinese economy and financial system facing?
A $3.5 trillion drop in stock market capitalization does not necessarily mean the economy has lost a corresponding amount of cash. However, if stock prices continue to fall while the real estate market and corporate profits have not recovered, the asset devaluation effect could make households more cautious in their spending, while also undermining business and investor confidence.

The credit system can also be affected if a company's ability to repay debt declines, the value of collateral decreases, and bad debts increase.
However, the decline in the stock market alone is not sufficient grounds to assess the risk of a banking or financial crisis in China. The assessment needs to be based on other factors, such as the asset quality of banks, the solvency of businesses, and developments in the real estate market.
Furthermore, China still has monetary and fiscal policy tools to support the economy and provide liquidity when needed. However, measures to support financial markets are unlikely to address the root causes of problems such as weak consumption, excess capacity, and declining corporate profits unless domestic demand improves significantly.
Therefore, the prospects for stock market recovery depend not only on measures to support stock prices, but also on the ability to restore consumer demand, stabilize the real estate market, and improve the business performance of enterprises.
China's biggest challenge is not just reviving its stock market, but also restoring domestic demand and improving corporate profits. Until these fundamentals recover significantly, the upward trend in stocks will be difficult to sustain.

“It is strange that the deputy prime minister is quarrelling with the secretary-general to the point of making the revelation publicly in Parliament.

“We do not want the people of Sabah and Sarawak to be confused and become victims,” he added.

The Umno president said his ministry ended up spending a total of RM6.108 billion in those three years, arguing that this meant it had in fact underspent.
